subsubtopic: ALLEGED MISREPRESENTATIONS IN TABLING OF REPORT-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to request the unanimous consent of the House to propose a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In the Votes and Proceedings of the House for October 8, 1971, No. 187, at page 864, under the heading "Returns and Reports Deposited with the Clerk of the House" appears the following purported record of a proceeding in this House:
By Mr. Chretien, a member of the Queen's Privy Council,- Report of the Northern Canada Power Commission for the year ended March 31, 1971, pursuant to section 24 of the Northern Canada Power Commission Act, chapter N-21, R.S.C., 1970, together with the accounts and financial statement certified by the Auditor General, pursuant to section 75(3) of the Financial Administration Act, chapter F-10, R.S.C., 1970.-Sessional Paper No. 283-1-196.
Mr. Speaker, this entry contains two allegations intended to mislead this House.
The first allegation is a misrepresentation of the law. The report purports to be made pursuant to section 24 of the Northern Canada Power Commission Act. The report was not tabled pursuant to section 24: the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the officers of the commission violated the law by failing to file a return as required by that section.
The second wrongful allegation is a misstatement of fact. The Auditor General, an officer of this House, did not certify the accounts and financial statement of the
commission pursuant to section 75(3) of the Financial Administration Act. On the contrary, he advised the minister:
Due to the continuing unsatisfactory condition of the records, I am unable to express an opinion as required by section 77 of the Financial Administration Act on the validity of either the accounts or the financial statements for the year ended March 31, 1971.
There also appear to be other violations of the law by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and by the officers-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLEGED MISREPRESENTATIONS IN TABLING OF REPORT-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext: Order, please. As the hon. member knows, the purpose of this Standing Order is that all members may have the opportunity to move a motion in very special circumstances without the 48-hour notice normally required under the Standing Orders. The interpretation of this section is that hon. members have to indicate briefly why there is urgency and what the motion is. I suggest to hon. members and to the hon. member for the Yukon that the Standing Order does not make it possible for hon. members to make lengthy statements in support of a motion. I am sure the hon. member will want to take that into account and indicate as soon as possible what the motion is that he proposes for the unanimous consent of the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the only reason I felt that it should be a little more detailed than usual under Standing Order 43 was that two officers of this House were involved, namely, the Clerk of this House and the Auditor General. In any event, I had almost completed the sentence, the rest of it being-of the commission as detailed by the Auditor General in paragraph 131 of his report for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1970. I therefore propose to move, seconded by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin):
That the report of the Northern Canada Power Commission for the year ended March 31, 1971, deposited in this House on the 8th October 1971, as Sessional Paper No. 283-1-196, be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs to inquire into violations of law by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the responsible past and present officers of the commission in their conduct and management of the affairs of the Commission; and, as well, to inquire into violations of the rules, practices and conventions of this House with respect to the depositing of the said report in this House; and to report to this House, as quickly as possible, its findings and recommendations.
And that it be an order of this House that, pending the report of the committee and further order by this House thereon, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development be suspended from the service of this House; and that this House urge the government to suspend the officers of the Northern Canada Power Commission from their duties in the Public Service and place the conduct and management of the commission under the Auditor General of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43 I ask the unanimous consent of the House to propose a motion for the purpose of discussing a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, namely, the escalation of the school boycott by Indian students in northeastern Alberta. The issue has been aggravated this past weekend by the supportive action of another reserve, bringing the total number of students now being withheld to 1,600. This action, if allowed to continue, may very well escalate into a province-wide walk out, since today the chiefs of 43 Alberta bands are meeting to discuss further courses of action.

subtopic: CLEAN AIR ACT-ESTABLISHMENT OF AIR SAMPLING STATIONS
CLEAN AIR ACT-ESTABLISHMENT OF AIR SAMPLING STATIONS
speechtext:
1.	Following passage of the Clean Air Act, have any new sampling stations been added to the national surveillance network and, if so, how many?
2.	Are additional funds being allocated for the work of the air sampling program?

speakeroldname: Mr. Eymard Corbin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: CLEAN AIR ACT-ESTABLISHMENT OF AIR SAMPLING STATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, new stations are being added continuously to our National Air Pollution Surveillance Network. This program has been accelerating since January, 1970. This past summer, for example, we have added stations in both Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland as well as the province of Quebec. Our coverage as of this date is 237 sampling instruments in 36 cities across all ten provinces. This reflects a substantial improvement over the situation on January, 1970 when the coverage consisted of 128 instruments, 20 cities, and seven provinces.
The answer to the second part of the question is yes. Additional funds are being allocated to the air sampling program as well as to the whole of the air pollution control program as a result of passage of the Clean Air Act. These additional funds will be reflected in supplementary estimates for next year and in the main estimates for next year as part of my department's environmental quality program.

subtopic: COMPENSATION TO SWORDFISH INDUSTRY OF CANADA
speechtext:

speechtext:
Orders of the day.
[DOT] <3:00 p.m.)

The House resumed, from Wednesday, October 13, consideration in committee of Bill C-259, to amend the Income Tax Act and to make certain provisions and alterations in the statute law related to or consequential upon the amendments to that act-Mr. Benson-Mr. Boulanger in the chair.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate at this stage of the debate on the proposals for tax reform, I want to raise certain objections for the consideration of the Minister of Finance and his officials, I hope there is still time to correct what I believe to be an inequitable situation as it affects various aspects of community life within the constituency that I represent. My time is limited and I may have more comments to make later, but at the moment I wish to deal with one or two items in the hope that they may be elaborated upon when other members rise to speak.
There are many objectionable areas in the present proposal. In rural areas where farm incomes are low, not many farmers in the past have had to use chartered accountants to prepare their income tax returns. Over the years they had become accustomed to completing the forms themselves and were able to do so at a minimum cost. The present proposals with regard to evaluation day for property make things so complicated that farmers may find it necessary to turn to professionals for help. I can easily realize why the Minister of Finance would want to establish such a system. As an accountant himself, he has to do something for his friends and this is one way of giving them a little bit of the windfall he would have liked
October 18. 1971

to have when he was in business. Of course, after this reform it may happen that he will be back in the accounting business himself.
I, personally, have strong objections to the concept of a capital gains tax. I realize that my party has come out for it to a limited degree. But many parts of my constituency are only 25 or 30 years old, and I do not believe this type of area will be best served by the introduction of a capital gains tax. Indeed, I think it will be a deterrent, a mistake, but I will not dwell too long on that aspect. I know that members of the NDP feel the capital gains tax does not go far enough. Of course, you cannot convince them that anyone who is in business is not a millionaire or a multimillionaire, that there are many people in business who do not make vast fortunes. For some reason the NDP feels that you must go after anybody who calls himself a company or a corporation.
In the end, I believe the people to be hurt are those who the government is professing to help. Let me examine one aspect which is very discriminatory as far as the farmer is concerned. The new proposals provide that a home on one acre of ground shall be exempt. This is fine for people living in cities and towns but when we compare a city home with a farm home is there any equity in this form of taxation? Certainly, there is not. Anyone who has ever looked at the real estate section of a newspaper realizes that city homes have appreciated in value, in fact, have skyrocketed. Many homes in Toronto and Vancouver are worth $50,000 or $60,000 but how many in the rural areas are worth that much? In the magazine section of the Ottawa Citizen last weekend, there was an article which pointed out that lots in the Vancouver area are valued at $15,000 to $20,000. But the Minister of Finance should consider that a home on a quarter section of land in the west might be comparable to a lot which is usually less than an acre. An acre of land within city limits could be worth as much as a million dollars but there is not much farmland that would sell for a million dollars an acre.
I know that the minister is comparing like with like, home with home or acre with acre but he is certainly not comparing value with value. I concede that it is always going to be difficult to have equity. In the west where land is divided by quarter section or section or in acres, any deed you hold is to land which has not been subdivided. A lot has been subdivided. In cities many homes of 50 years of age have and will appreciate because of the shortage of housing. In the country a home can cost $20,000 but because of a reduction in family size and the changing pattern of education as well as the deterioration of community life, large homes are no longer being built. The value of the home on the farm may go down, whereas the value of the city home goes up. That distinction must be drawn and the minister ought to consider it. After all, what can a man do with an acre of land? Is he to incur the legal costs of subdividing an acre?
It could be that a farmer has built at $15,000 home on a $10,000 parcel of land to which he has title. That is quite possible. In any event, consideration must be given to that parcel of land on which the farm home is built. In some cases, land values have gone up and homes have appreciated. It may be that land values will continue
Income Tax Act
climbing. At the same time, I think that the suggestion I am making is a fairer and more equitable way of looking at this question. I realize that the minister is to allow annual depreciation of $1,000 against the home. At the same time, it must be realized that in many cases the farmer has to trade-off some of his land simply to stay in business. If the minister wishes to be fair, he will leave open to farmers the option with respect to that $1,000 annual depreciation in home value. In any event, the amount of revenue the government will lose in these cases will not be great.
In the few minutes remaining, I wish to touch on several other areas, including co-operatives. I have received representations in that regard. In also wish to touch on lumbering, which affects my area, and mining. There is one other aspect applying to farmers that I shall touch on.
I wish to talk about the accrual system of depreciation. I believe the minister should allow either the accrual system or the straight-line system of depreciation. If he maintains that the accrual system should be used, he ought to realize that only in the first two years will the accrual system be of advantage to a farmer, and only if the farmer buys a new machine. That is, the system will bring advantages in the calculation of income tax. Yet I ask, how many farmers are in a position to trade their machinery every two years? Not very many, I suggest. Usually, if a farmer trades within two years, he has bought a lemon and wishes to get rid of it. In that case he will take a loss, anyway. If that farmer wants to remain efficient, and that is the aspect to which the government has failed to give consideration, he must trade his machinery when necessary. I submit that under the accrual system the farmer will simply delay trading his machinery. He will try to get as much out of it as possible in write-off benefits. Yet, if he holds on to his machinery for too long, his efficiency will suffer.
Look at it another way, Mr. Chairman. If a farmer has great sales in one year, he will certainly not trade his machinery in that year if he has at his disposal unused accumulated depreciation benefits, because that unused depreciation will be charged against his income tax if he trades. So, he must wait for a year in which his sales are low. That year, when he ought to tighten his belt, will be the only time he can write off the accumulated depreciation against income tax. Because of his low return in that year, he can use the unused portion of his accrued depreciation and write it off in that year. That is to say, he will have to add the unused portion of his depreciation to his income tax. That is what will happen under the accrual system. So, the farmer will not trade in the good year but must wait for a bad year. This approach defies all logic. Would any banker grant you a loan if you told him you have had a bad year? Would he not say to you, "What's the matter with you, man; get with it and tighten your belt. You should not take out a loan this year because you may have another bad year next year." Yet that is precisely the position the farmer will be in if the minister adopts the accrual system as against the straightline system, as proposed.
Page 6 of the brief of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture reads:
The fact is that in farming income is typically low in relation to investment, obsolescence is rapid, inflation of farmers costs con-

October 18, 1971
Income Tax Act
tinues year after year, and more expensive and sophisticated machinery, equipment and structures have to be constantly introduced into the business.
The Federation suggests that the farmers should be allowed to retain the option of depreciating assets on a straightline basis. They go on to say, as recorded on page 7, that they believe farmers must:
Be able to maintain a separate bookkeeping on assets acquired up to December 13-71 on the present straightline basis, with assets subsequently purchased separately set up on a diminishing balance basis.. . . That capital gains if any, be calculated on the difference between disposition price and original cost or Valuation Day value, whichever is the higher.
I will go even farther than the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and suggest that either system ought to be allowed. One must realize that farmers have constantly struggled to maintain efficiency, and we should not deprive them of any leeway in that regard. Farmers, I think, have been fairly good businessmen over the years and have tried, whenever possible, to remain in business. I do not think that hemming them in under an accrual system will work to their advantage or to the advantage of the industry, as a whole.
Another aspect that I wish to cover, if I have time, relates to the basic herd concept. Mr. Chairman, it takes years and years to build up a basic herd. Yet you can dispose of that herd in one easy sale. All you must do is order a truck to pick up the herd and take it to market, and that is the end of your herd which has taken years and years to establish. The Federation of Agriculture deals with this. They believe that a herd should be treated as capital. I think there would be an advantage to farmers if the minister were to treat the herd as capital. As I have already pointed out, it takes years to establish a herd. Also, you can dispose of the herd in one easy sale. I realize that the averaging concept may come into play. Yet averaging could be useful for only four or five years if you have had a series of setbacks after a period of good years.
One must also consider the case of the farmer who, for reasons of health, must dispose of his cattle or capital. Possibly the farmer and his son have been working together, and perhaps the son has been doing most of the manual work. Perhaps the son finds that they cannot carry on the business, and they must therefore dispose of the herd. I think the minister ought to look at this matter on the basis of previously calculated income tax or on the basis of future income tax that may be calculated. I think he ought to consider the 20 or 25 years it may have taken to build up a herd of this type. The minister ought to take all this into consideration.
I now wish to touch briefly on co-operatives. Many people in my riding have had experience with co-operatives or credit unions.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.
Continue.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member may continue only with the unanimous consent of the committee. Is there such unanimous consent?
Agreed.

I thank the committee, Mr. Chairman. I will be very brief. I only want to deal briefly with the "co-op" aspect of the proposal. Many co-operatives have been established to service a local need. I agree with this concept. I have done my share of work in this field. I think the objection which is made by members of the co-operative movement with regard to double taxation is valid. Although the minister has introduced some amendments, the Co-operative Union of Canada does not think they go far enough to meet their requirements. Perhaps the minister may wish at this time or some time in the future to exempt the .local co-operatives, since they serve a local need.
Some co-operatives have become large monopolies. They were established in earlier days to cut down on the unfairness and unethical practices of some individuals. They have served a need. Once they become large corporations, they are somewhat of a nightmare to many small businessmen in the communities. In some instances they speed up the day when small communities become depleted. Once communities are depleted, it is only through the co-operatives that any type of service can be maintained or sustained. At that time no enterpriser will go into the community because he fears he will lose money on the venture. Many co-operatives are established as a result.
In the interest of maintaining some form of service in the small communities, the minister should look upon co-operatives as small enterprises. They should be kept separate from the large enterprises. In so doing, the minister will meet some of the objections which the small businessmen have to the co-operative idea. At the same time, the minister must realize that we have to maintain the small credit unions in communities where the banks have failed to help the local businessmen and farmers. In cases where the banks simply refuse to make loans on the basis of past experience, the credit unions have often done so. The interest rate may be higher for that reason.
I will not take up any more of the time of the committee. I again thank the committee for having allowed me a few extra minutes. I may elaborate on these points at a later time.

Mr. Chairman, I make no claim to having read every word of the 707 page bill which the minister has placed before us for consideration. I make no apology for that at this point because it seems that this mammoth bill is largely the result of the inconsistency of the government's approach to fair taxation. Had the government seen fit to put before this House the basic principles of the royal commission report, commonly referred to as the Carter report, we could have had a much less extensive and more readily understandable bill than the one we are considering today.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Would you have read it?

However, the choice has been that of the government and this is the bill we have to consider. I rise this afternoon to deal with one aspect of the bill. The hon. member who preceded me touched on this aspect in his

October 18, 1971_____________________COMMONS DEBATES	8777
closing remarks. I will not attempt to take quite the same line of attack as he did.
I suppose other hon. members received, as I did, a letter from the Co-operative Union of Canada dated October 15, 1971. I wish to put the contents of this letter on record. The letter, addressed to Members of the House of Commons, reads as follows:
Since we wrote to you on September 20th, the government has introduced amendments to Section 135 of Bill C-259 relating to the taxation of co-operatives.
Co-operatives wish to advise you these amendments do not meet the objections of co-operatives.
Co-operatives insist that the fundamental distinction in their nature be respected by the taxation statute. These distinctions are:
(a)	the co-operative provides primarily a self-help service required by its members.
(b)	the co-operative distributes its earnings to its members in proportion to member business.
(c)	the co-operative raises and "services" its equity capital by revolving the same in relation to the use of the co-operative by its members.
(d)	the capital contributed by a member of the co-operative is to provide himself with services and not to produce a return on investment.
Co-operatives request that they be permitted to distribute the income from member business to their members as a patronage refund as is intended by their charters, bylaws and nature with no limitation. These distributions, of course, will be dealt with by the members in their personal taxable income in a manner similar to the distributions of the earning of a partnership to its members.
Yours sincerely,
W. B. Melvin, President, on behalf of Co-operative Union of Canada and Le Conseil canadien de la Cooperation
As a member of this House, I say at once that I stand four-square behind the statement submitted by the president of the Co-operative Union of Canada. It is little short of disgraceful that a government which calls itself Liberal and sometimes expresses a desire for a free society in this country, should, by a taxation law, seek to twist and distort the basic freedom of co-operatives to operate as co-operatives. This is the issue that has to be joined at this point.
There is a lot of talk from time to time by various political spokesmen in this country about what is referred to as free enterprise. If we are going to have freedom of enterprise, there should be freedom of enterprise. The citizens of Canada who decide they wish to band together as a non-profit organization to operate as a co-operative should be allowed to do so. The Minister of Finance has no moral right to place a tax bill before this House which negates the basic principles of co-operatives. This is what he is obviously doing, as one can see by referring to the letter from the president of the Co-operative Union of Canada.
What would Carter have done?

That is a very good question. If the principles of the Carter commission report had been followed, this sort of nonsense about co-operatives would not be before us. The Carter commission recommended, in effect, that we move toward doing away with the complicated system of taxing income in the hands of corporations and again in the hands of individuals. As far as the corporation tax is concerned, the government has rejected
Income Tax Act
that principle. It is trying to suck the co-operatives into the basket, and that is why I say that was a very good question.
At the outset of my remarks, I said that if the government had brought in a tax bill based upon the principles of the Carter commission report, we would not be indulging in this silly nonsense of trying to twist, squirm and appease the multitudinous members of co-operatives. I want to make it clear that I, as an individual, and the party to which I belong, as a matter of policy accept the principle that co-operatives should be encouraged to develop freely along the lines on which they were organized. We should not seek to twist and distort the basic principles of the co-operative movement with income tax laws like the one presently before us, even with the so-called concessions the minister has put before the House. I have been a member of consumer co-operatives for many years.
I, and other members, recognize the fact that the credit unions are essentially co-operatives in the business of lending money. They operate on the same basis. The credit unions have placed their position before us along much the same lines as have the co-operative unions. One of the briefs which has been received has come from the Ontario Credit Union movement. I have a copy here of a letter which was addressed to me under date of October 4, 1971 by the Ontario Credit Union League. They raise this question of what constitutes fair taxation. They point out that there is held an inaccurate opinion that there are tax concessions made to credit unions. I have received for a number of years, now, a lot of drivel from this so-called Equitable Tax Foundation which has been trying to argue that co-operatives and credit unions are receiving special tax concessions. I have looked at it, and then done what I thought was appropriate-I put it in the waste basket. Apparently the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has been sucked in by this sort of drivel and propaganda. I suppose one should not be too surprised at that. It is a symptom of the type of hodge-podge Liberal policies so often wind up as being.
Let us not be fooled by the amendments the minister has suggested should be made to the bill. The president of the co-operative union has placed the issue squarely before us and I, as one member of this House, am prepared to stand behind that position with the support, I believe, of every member of my party. We do not want any of this weaseling and squirming, this effort to appease the credit unions and the co-operatives on the one hand and the private corporations on the other hand. Members of our party have admitted from time to time in various debates there is a place in what is sometimes called a mixed economy for the private profit making type of enterprise. We have never said we intend to abolish it or discriminate against it. But we have also said we believe there is a place for the co-operative type of enterprise, that it should be allowed to operate freely and be available to those who wish to use it in its varying forms and manifestations. So I wish to register my strong protest against the bill we have before us, even with the suggested amendments which are apparently to be foisted upon the co-operative movements unless somehow we can per-

suade the majority of members of this House to reject the proposals of the government in this field as they stand.

Mr. Chairman, I have spoken several times on the general principles embodied in the legislation with which we are now dealing. I have expressed the opinion that what we have before us is not by any stretch of the imagination tax reform but simply tax change; that the tinkering the government proposes is mere tinkering and that the inequities of our tax system as outlined by the Carter Commission, which made it very clear that the people in the lower income brackets are paying substantially more in tax than they ought to pay, and that the people in the middle and upper income brackets are paying substantially less, will continue after this proposed revision of our tax system.
I wish to deal specifically today with one matter which has been raised with some success, but not enough, by the co-operatives and credit union movement. Unfortunately, after the government tabled its white paper in response to the Carter Commission Report, and after the minister brought in his bill, unfortunately, but not too surprisingly, the vast bulk of the representations which were made to the minister and to the parliamentary committee which dealt with the white paper and the bill on taxation came from those who had the ability, the knowledge and the money to hire experts to make the representations outlining the complaints which they felt should be made, namely, the business community, the self-employed people who felt that the minor changes which the minister first proposed in his white paper and the even smaller changes which he proposed in his tax bill, went too far. The vast bulk of the people, the ordinary people, the wage and salary-earners who pay every penny of income tax which the law requires them to pay, who have no way of making deductions for expenses or trips or anything else, were not able to make representations.
They did it in Winnipeg last week, did they not?

It is an interesting development we see in regard to the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Osier). When he was running as a candidate he was careful to try to create the impression that he was just an ordinary citizen like everybody else. But since he has come down here, increasingly we find in his interjections and in his speeches-and I do not mind them, because he usually puts his foot into his mouth-that the real person comes out. He is from one of the few top families in Winnipeg. They've got it made, and he is going to keep on seeing that they are protected. That is the kind of interjections we get from him.
I asked you whether it was only rich people who gave you the gears in Winnipeg last week.

I shall be happy to discuss the principle of this bill. If the hon. member will stop interjecting he will not get the kind of replies which his interjections deserve.
The one group which made representations, and very strong representations, to the minister, to other cabinet ministers and to every Member of Parliament, was the co-operative and credit unions. They made their views known strongly. Let me quote from a press release put out some time ago by the United Co-operatives of Ontario with regard to the proposals contained in this bill:
Upon careful study of the proposed tax legislation presented to the ways and means committee, the Co-operative Union of Canada finds that compliance with these proposals will create extreme difficulties for- co-operatives. The net result will be to force cooperatives to abandon their basic nature-
The Co-operative Union of Canada feels it is not the prerogative of a taxation body to interfere with the relationship between an organization and its members. The taxation imposed should be in keeping with the nature of the taxpayer. The proposed legislation totally disregards objections raised in the Co-operative Union's submission to Mr. Benson and to the taxation committee of the House of Commons and of the Senate.
The proposals failed to take into consideration the basic nature and method of operation of a co-operative, which is to distribute surplus earnings to members in proportion to the business they have done with their co-op rather than in relation to capital investment.
Co-operative philosophy, regulations, etc. make it impractical for most co-ops to distribute their surplus earnings as proposed. Further the proposals failed to recognize the difference between the nature of equity capital employed by co-operatives and by other corporations.
If there is one group that has done a great deal to protect the ordinary citizen, it is the credit union. This is the one organization that protects not the Member of Parliament, the businessman, the doctor or lawyer, who can usually go the bank and arrange a loan if they get into financial difficulty, but the ordinary citizens who do not have much income or any collateral to offer as security for a loan from the bank and who in increasing numbers are being forced to go to the loan companies.
I am not going to criticize the loan companies. They are not breaking any law in this country; they are fulfilling a function that no other organization with the exception of the credit union has been fulfilling. But the loan companies have been doing so at exorbitant cost, to say the least. They have been acting legally but, in my view, unconscionably, lending money to citizens in this country at interest rates of 18, 24, 30 per cent per annum. Anyone who doubts this needs only look at the interest rates charged by finance companies on the purchase of automobiles. No one can argue today that an automobile is any longer a luxury; it has become a necessity in this country. The one organization that has stood between the loan companies-the "loan sharks"-and the ordinary citizens is the credit union. If any government brought in any legislation that would destory the credit unions, it was the original bill brought in by the Minister of Finance.
As a result of representations made by the co-operatives and credit unions to Members of Parliament and the government, the minister has announced a series of amendments, I think 95 in all, to this bill. Nevertheless, today I was in touch with representatives of the credit
October 18, 1971

unions in this country, and while they are pleased with some of the changes and agree that some of the amendments that the minister introduced go part of the way to overcoming the problems the original bill created for them, they made it very clear that there are still some sections of the bill that must be amended. If they are not amended, then the ability of the credit unions to function, to grow and to give the kind of protection they have been giving increasingly to thousands of Canadians who need this organization will be jeopardized.
Let me put on the record the comments which the representatives of the credit unions made to me today in the hope that it is not too late and that the Minister of Finance will demonstrate that he does sometimes listen not only to the representations made by mining, gas and oil companies but also those made by ordinary citizens. Perhaps within the next few days the minister will add another couple of amendments to the 95 he has already tabled so as to take care of the difficulties created by this legislation for the credit unions.
The officials from the credit unions have told me that the section of the bill dealing with the opening reserve that will be established on January 1, 1972, as now drafted, leaves a good deal to be desired. The government proposes to allow credit unions reserves similar to those held by banks. The credit unions are concerned about what will happen to the statutory reserves they are required to hold and maintain by the provinces, and about whether they will be taxed retroactively. The credit unions are asking that they be allowed to begin the taxation year in January 1972 at point zero; in other words, that their prior reserves that have been built up under the requirements of provincial legislation be ignored so that new reserves can be accumulated, as is the case with other corporations. I want to make it clear that the credit unions are not asking for any special consideration but that they be given the same treatment as other corporations.
The credit unions are concerned about one other important aspect of the tax legislation, and this is the small business limit concept. Credit unions will not be permitted to take advantage of the small business limit concept. Small business, under the proposal made by the minister, will be permitted to set aside reserves of $50,000 a year which will be taxed at the low rate of 25 per cent rather than the usual 50 per cent. Credit unions, as they understand it, will not be permitted to do this because the reserve funds required by the provinces are locked in and therefore cannot be distributed to the members. Since the credit unions will be unable to distribute any dividends to the members, they will not be able to reduce their taxable income.
I think that what the credit unions want is fairly simple to understand and is a very fair request to make. They want the same tax incentives that are now allowed small business. Although credit unions are large organizations with many thousands of members, I would imagine that, in 99.9 per cent of the cases, those members are in a much poorer financial position than the small businessman who will be permitted a lower tax rate. As I say, the credit unions are asking for the same kind of treatment in the matter of taxation that small businesses will be permitted

under this legislation, and as I say it is not too late for the minister to bring in a further amendment that will give the credit unions this kind of treatment. No proposal that I know of was greeted with such unanimous criticism by the credit unions and co-operatives as the original proposal made by the minister. I hope the minister will do something pretty substantial to meet what I consider to be the very legitimate concerns of the credit unions and co-operatives in respect of this legislation.
I should like to deal with just one more matter before I sit down and that is my feeling that the minister, while appearing to try to meet the needs of ordinary citizens in a much more equitable manner by raising income tax exemptions from $1,000 to $1,500 for a single person and from $2,000 to $2,850 for married couples, in fact has not come anywhere close to meeting what the situation was when the $1,000 per single person and $2,000 per married person basic exemption was put into the legislation more than 20 years ago. Need I remind the minister of the tremendous increase in the cost of living in the past 22 years since that floor was set for calculating income tax exemption? Need I remind the minister that under his proposal there will be tens of thousands, probably hundreds of thousands of Canadian citizens who will be paygngihcome taxi7evem7though,i7according to thecalcula-tions of the Economic Council of Canada, they are in fact living in poverty?
It seems to me that there is something wrong in principle, and something cruel, about a government in the year 1971 proposing that people who are living in poverty should be required to pay any income tax. I urge the minister to adopt the proposals put forward by organizations such as those representing the pensioners who have suggested that the minimum basic exemption in calculating income tax should be $2,000 a year for a single person and $4,000 a year for a married one. I know that the minister has been very adept at putting on the record again and again, the fact that hundreds of thousands of people will no longer have to pay income tax when the new schedule and the new exemptions which he is proposing are put into effect. But the minister has been very careful not to explain to the public how little income tax is paid by those who will now be exempt, a few dollars a year. Of course it is good that they should not be paying it, but those people should not have been paying income tax for years. What the minister has done is in fact too little and too late.
The minister has done the same kind of public relations job, the same kind of snow job, as he did the other day when he announced in his package of last Thursday that in order to try to get the economy moving, the economy which he has been saying has been doing very well, in order to reduce unemployment, there would be a cut of 3 per cent in income tax. An across-the-board cut for the person with a taxable income of $4,000 or $5,000 a year comes to a few cents a week. To the person earning $20,000 a year or $30,000 a year a 3 per cent cut in income tax is a very substantial amount of money. So, last Thursday the minister did what he has done on nearly every occasion on which, when I have heard him make a

proposal for change, he has given more to those who already have than to those who do not have.
May I express this last plea to the minister before I sit down, that the minister give serious consideration to wiping out the kind of restrictive proposals in this tax legislation which he originally proposed for co-operatives and credit unions; that he meet their very reasonable suggestion that their task of looking after their members, who are on the whole very ordinary citizens in the moderate income brackets, be not made more difficult than it has been and that he do things to help them to get more members and to expand their services to those people who really need the kind of service which they perform; and also that the minister give serious and favourable consideration to raising basic exemptions on income tax so that those people who cannot afford to pay income tax, people in the lower income brackets earning less than $2,000 a year and family people earning less than $4,000 a year, not be required to pay any income tax at all.

Mr. Chairman, one of the features of Bill C-259 would eliminate an exemption which hitherto has existed with respect to prospectors. I want to devote some of my remarks this afternoon to the impact that this proposed legislation will have on the mining industry generally and on the oil and gas industries. Perhaps the place to start is where most new mines start, with the hard work and dedication of the individual prospector. As was pointed out in the letter by the management of the British Columbia and Yukon Chamber of Mines to the Prime Minister on September 1 last, the fact has been clearly established that:
-prospectors are vitally important to the future of our mineral industry. You will note that prospectors in British Columbia-Yukon have been responsible for discovering at least 1,377 million tons of ore valued at $8,605 million, and that it would take 97,000 man years of work to extract the ore. In other words, a great many jobs for Canadians over a period of many years.
Bill C-259 would abolish the existing exemption of prospectors so that the proceeds of their efforts, if they ever do realize them, are free of tax. That was not the attitude, however, of the standing committee because in its final report dealing with the white paper on taxation the committee recommended that prospectors be exempted from this tax. Unfortunately, not only the Minister of Finance but the government did not see fit to accept the recommendations of the standing committee. However, that is not surprising and it is another indication of the so-called reform of the committee system and how useless it is. The mining industry in Canada has become the country's most important industry, accounting for perhaps more than 40 per cent of Canada's export dollars, with well over 25 Canadian communities being entirely dependent upon the industry, and in the north, not only whole communities but in the case of the Yukon the whole of that geographic entity, is dependent almost entirely and absolutely on a healthy and viable mining industry. The industry is a little over 100 years old and already it consists of some 240 or more producing mines. Several briefs were presented to the standing committee when the whitepaper proposals were considered. One of the best, and perhaps one of the most humorous, was the brief presented by Dean Vaughan who heads a group of prospectors from Toronto. He says on page two of that brief-and I believe this is actual-

ly what happened in respect of one of the proposals in Bill C-259-if this country were secretly invaded by hostile Martians intent on crippling the Canadian economy, they would be very well advised to infiltrate our government and politically cripple the mining industry, which has created for the Canadian economy more than $40 billion in new wealth in the past 25 years. And then he asked, how better could these Martian politicians, under the guise of tax reform and social reform, sabotage the third largest mining industry in the world. He suggests a timetable by which that sabotage could be carried on by the federal government. He says that the leader, in this case he would be the Minister of Finance, would recommend to his superiors, the Prime Minister and his government, the following program.
The first item would be to tax new mining ventures to death before they are on their feet. That is exactly what these proposals will accomplish. Instead of waiting until new mines are in production and contributing to the wealth of the country, we are going to start taxing them before these mines are even discovered by imposing a tax on the potential gains of the prospector, a prospector who in some cases has been searching for mineral deposits for some 20 years, or a quarter of a century, and who may never realize anything from his efforts. Certainly, the odds are highly against any single prospector hitting it twice.
The second step in Mr. Vaughan's program would be to immobilize the self-employed prospector by cutting off his supply of risk capital via the imposition of a capital gains tax on money won by the prospector and his grubstakers. That is exactly what happens now. It takes a good deal of persuasion to convince hard-headed business persons to invest in such a high risk venture as a prospector or grubstaking a prospector in the search for new mines. A prospector can promise nothing but hard work and, usually in my part of the country in any event, a very short season. There is no guarantee to the investor that he will have any return on his high risk investment.
The third step suggested in the program is to harass the mining industry as a whole by enacting emotional, hasty and retroactive restrictions in an otherwise free economy. Again, that is what the proposals in Bill C-259 are aimed at. The fourth step suggested is to conspire to establish a lack of confidence within the country and throughout the mining industry, not only here but outside our borders, and in the minds of foreign investors regarding future socialistic and jingoistic political ambitions.
In a report produced recently for the British Columbia Mining Association by an internationally recognized firm of chartered accountants, Prince, Waterhouse, it is estimated that the investment capital inflow in mining activities in the Yukon in 1970 after the publication of the white paper proposals was reduced by 72 per cent over the preceding year. The white paper on taxation and the proposal to replace the Yukon Quartz Mining Act with Bill C-187, the Yukon Minerals Act and the Land Use Regulations, combine to scare off investment capital to that extent and I daresay to the same extent this year. Unless some relief is forthcoming, and unless we have some statement from the Minister of Indian Affairs and
October 18, 1971

Northern Development and from the Minister of Finance, we face a more bleak year ahead so far as exploration activity in the Yukon is concerned during the season of 1972.
As a fifth step in his program of sabotaging the industry, Mr. Vaughan suggests the introduction of prejudicial legislation regarding foreign ownership; for example, England may control Canadian uranium mines but the United States may not. We have seen the reaction across the border with regard to the restrictive legislation that has been imposed with regard to the inflow of capital investment into this country from south of the border. This government is in deep trouble with regard to its relations with the United States. It is inconceivable that there could have been such rapid deterioration of our Canada-United States relations in so short a time. Investor confidence in the United States so far as investment in our mineral and resource industries is concerned has hit a new low. This is one reason we find our economic plight in the Yukon so desperate and why we have so little to look forward to during the forthcoming season. This is an industry which is highly risky so far as investment capital is concerned. It is an industry which, instead of having restrictive provisions such as are proposed in Bill C-259 and C-187, should be given incentives.
The sixth point in Mr. Vaughan's program for sabotaging the industry would be to sell foreign investors and companies mining exploration permits under one set of rules, then change the rules in the middle of the game and then change the rules back again. For example, look at what happened to Gulf Oil at Woollaston Lake and Phillips Petroleum and Atlantic Richfield in the Arctic. We have a good example of that in the intention of the government to include a power to make regulations in Bill C-187. That fits hand in glove with the powers which will exist under the legislation before us and also the power under the Territorial Lands Act under which all oil and gas exploration permits are granted.
The seventh step in the program would be to impose sweeping uneconomic legislation restricting the disposal or sale of concentrates or mining products with no industry-wide dialogue or advanced notice. That is precisely what was proposed in Bill C-187 where the minister would have absolute control over any ore exported from the country in excess of I believe 5,000 tons. I could be mistaken on that figure. In other words it was not management of the mining industry by the investors and shareholders but rather was management of the industry by the government. This is state control over an industry which has enjoyed its spectacular growth as a result of incentives and freedoms in the past.
As a final step in his program to sabotage the mining industry, Mr. Vaughan suggests we impose a recurring five-year reassessment of capital gains tax, with all its attendant catastrophic implications. If there is one area where capital gains should not apply it is in the area of the gains which are achieved by the prospector who discovers the mines in the first place. Any member of this committee who has knowledge of or personal acquaintanceship with prospectors, knows the hardships which these individuals must endure, for the most part over many,
Income Tax Act
many years, before they realize anything from their efforts.
It is said, not only by the Minister of Finance but by his colleague, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, that technology has rendered the prospector obsolete. I submit that this is not so, and that new mines and new mineral prospects continue to be discovered by the prospector in the initial instance. Why should a Canadian in the position of a prospector who works for 20 years or a quarter of a century,-I know several in this category who have spent their money and efforts over the course of those long, arduous years-and who happens to become successful, wind up paying a tax on the gain that he might make from his participation in a producing mine?
As I pointed out a moment ago, in the last 100 years there were 240 mines discovered. Assuming an individual prospector was responsible for each individual discovery, what real gain does the government get from taxing 240 individual prospectors, instead of adopting the approach of giving them some incentives to discover new mineral prospects in the hope that they can bring new mines into production. Certainly, the government will derive more revenue from taxing new producing mines and from taxing all the employees of those mines than from taxing the individual prospectors.
There are several factors in the fiscal approach of the government which are scaring off investment capital from minerals. We might ask ourselves why some of the greatest incentives for hunting oil and gas in Canada are not created by Ottawa, by our fiscal measures, or by any fiscal measures adopted in the provinces, but actually come from Washington, for Americans? Why is it that Canadians are not prone to invest in the development of their own country, in one of the greatest single areas where development would be welcomed, and in fact is needed? Why does U.S. capital come across in greater volume than it comes from within our own country? I suggest that despite the new tax reforms proposed in Bill C-259 the greatest incentives for hunting oil and gas in Canada will continue to come from Washington for Americans, and not from the provinces or from Ottawa.
When the past minister of communications resigned from the federal cabinet he did not lose much time in expressing his dissatisfaction with our present economic policies. One key are of his discontent was that Canada's mismanagement of its natural resources and the apparently favourable tax climate in which natural resource companies operate, were to our detriment. In fact natural resource companies, such as those in the Canadian oil and gas industry, are severely handicapped in Canada by existing tax laws. I cannot bring myself to agree with the position that is taken by members of the NDP. It simply bespeaks an ignorance or lack of information on this subject, and I say that with great respect. Tax laws in the United States make it easier for foreign owned companies to operate in Canada, and they are also one of the main reasons why much of Canada's oil and gas industry is owned by companies in the United States.

The key to a successful oil and gas operation is the productivity of its exploration program, and that goes for the hard rock industry as well. Without exploration no minerals would be found. Without exploration no oil and gas would be found. That is certainly fundamental. Some of the greatest incentives for hunting oil and gas in Canada are not created here in this country, in Ottawa or in the provinces, but come from Washington for Americans. I want to illustrate this.
Under Canada's present tax laws no real incentive or encouragement is given to Canadians to participate in a risk taking venture. We have given them some meagre incentives which the government now wants to abolish. Quite to the contrary, however, American tax laws favour the use of essentially private capital in such ventures. These laws provide a means by which well to do Americans-by that I mean people with surplus capital who are looking for investment areas-can find relief from high taxes. I am going to discuss this by describing what the industry calls drilling funds.
A drilling fund is essentially a pool of risk taking money, collected from well off professionals such as doctors, lawyers, engineers and others who may be paying as much as 50 per cent of their top layer of income in tax. Millions of dollars are pouring into Canada from such U.S. drilling funds. The key to the success of the American drilling fund is that the fund guarantees, by virtue of U.S. law, a 92 per cent tax write off. On an initial investment of-

I thank members of the committee. I was discussing a drilling fund, and the fact that U.S. tax laws provide a 92 per cent tax write off for people fortunate enough to invest $10,000, $5,000, or whatever it may be in such a drilling fund. Let us take $10,000 as an example. $9,200 is deductible, and 8 per cent is commission on the purchase of fund units and is non-deductible. Thus the investor saves $4,600 in tax, making his net cost in that investment only $5,400.
If oil or gas is found, the investor has an additional source of income from the newly discovered oil or gas well. If he makes an annual income from the newly discovered well, of again let us say $10,000, he has to declare this additional income, which is taxable. However, this time the investor is given a 221 per cent depletion allowance, leaving a taxable income of only $7,750. If he reinvests the $7,750 in the drilling fund he can again get a 92 per cent write off, and now claims $3,875 as a tax write off. And so it goes. According to Art Klimchuck, who is a vice president of American Quasar Petroleum Co., only

167,000 of an estimated 2,600,000 U.S. taxpayers in the 50 per cent bracket have used such funds. Obviously, this kind of investment has barely touched its potential.
Two examples will illustrate the effect such a drilling fund has on Canada's oil and gas industry. The first is the Canadian-American Resources Fund Inc. (Can-Am), an offshoot of the previously mentioned American Quasar Petroleum Co. Each investor in Can-Am buys his participation in $5,000 units as a partner in a venture, not as a shareholder. Can-Am makes drilling money available to Quasar Petroleum Ltd. of Calgary, a Canadian subsidiary of American Quasar. The profits from this joint venture are split 60 per cent to the fund's partners and 40 per cent to Quasar. For the individual fund partner, success means income and failure means success because of a lighter tax burden through write-offs.
The second example is Husky Oil. According to Gene Roark, President of the Company, Husky was able to raise $32.5 million in the United States through its drilling fund at a time when the stock market was severely depressed. Much of this money will be spent in Canada on Husky's extensive nation-wide exploration program. Implementation of Bill C-259, as presently proposed, will continue to favour those elements in the tax structure that have led to the foreign domination of Canada's oil and gas industries. At a time when some public concern favours Canadian nationalism in this area, some serious changes are warranted that would at least provide parity incentives for Canadian investors in the oil and gas industries.
According to the views of the former minister of communications, the hon. member for Duvernay, it is quite true that natural resource companies in Canada enjoy a favoured tax position relative to other industries in Canada. This, however, is not the main point of contention; much more important than Canadian tax favours to natural resources companies is the fact that American companies operating in Canada enjoy an even more favoured position under American tax laws. If Canada is truly concerned about ownership of its own resources and the participation of Canadians in the development of Canada and is not using that ploy as a political straw man, then Bill C-259 will do little to foster these aims.
Perhaps the only solution to this problem is that tax laws in Canada should provide the same basis for at least a fair competition with foreign concerns. This objective could be achieved in one of two ways-provide a shelter for Canadian companies or change the tax laws so that they would provide a true incentive for Canadians to participate in risk ventures and the ultimate development of our own resources, regardless of the tax position of these industries relative to other industries in Canada. This is precisely the principle which I think the government is overlooking in the restrictions now being placed on this industry in Canada, not only the mining industry but the oil and gas industry as well.
Mr. Chairman, I have other submissions to make with respect to the principle of the bill as it affects the mining industry itself upon which I have not touched. I have spoken about the mining industry in which the prospector is going to be almost eliminated by Bill C-259 and one or

two aspects that affect the oil and gas industry, contrasting our laws and those of the United States. I have not touched on the hard rock industry and I propose to do that at another stage of these committee proceedings.

Mr. Chairman, I agree completely with what the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) had to say about prospecting. I well understand that people in his riding are interested in such activities. Some of my own electors are also highly interested, but I believe that prospectors have never been truly recognized by government authorities, whether provincial or federal. Prospectors have often been deprived of their rights, and the situation is the same today.
Recently, I mentioned, as an example, an incident that occurred in the federal riding of Villeneuve. A prospector named Lavoie had truly discovered a mine in Senneterre and, when the Department of National Defence decided to build a radar station there, the prospector was simply thrown out. His lands were nearly confiscated and the Department of National Defence failed to pay him any indemnity.
Mr. Chairman, with regard to prospecting, the government should, through Bill C-259, show greater generosity and a greater awareness of existing opportunities. In Northwestern Quebec, there are huge mining possibilities. However, the government failed to encourage prospecting. They did not omit to tax prospectors with incomes but they omitted to help them, to encourage them when they were in financial difficulties.
I agree with the comments of the hon. member for Yukon regarding prospectors and the possibility of developing new mines in our respective regions.
Bill C-259 is the natural result of the famous White Paper that has been so much talked about across Canada. The government has tried to put into concrete form the White Paper data in this Bill C-259 which is so complex that even chartered accountants are giving up trying to understand it. One accountant explains it one way, while another explains it another way. Even economists can't figure it out. It is so true that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) had to bring in 97 amendments to his own bill C-259. This means that nobody really understood what was meant by this reform of our present tax system.
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, fiscal reform brings about no increase in the total national income of Canadians. I suggest that Bill C-259 will be of little benefit to the poor. However, it will leave the rich practically unaffected whereas the middle class will be most directly hit.
People earning $8,000 to $60,000 a year are the ones who will offset tax reductions announced in regard to small wage-earners and those whose yearly incomes are very large.
It is therefore the middle class that Bill C-259 tends to eliminate and it has been followed by the announcement, a few days ago, of the famous program of winter works and government assistance to municipalities and provinces. In June last, when the Minister of Finance introduced his budget, he had to maintain surcharges and
Income Tax Act
special or temporary taxes. He now says that he is ready to reduce taxes in order to increase purchasing power and to undertake federal public works estimated at $1 billion.
This morning, I heard the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien)-I regret that he is not here-on the Frenchie Jarraud program in Montreal. Mr. Chairman, we do say that we should spread affluence instead of poverty among Canadians. If the Minister of Finance, in bill C-259, determined that any annual income under $5,000 for married people and under $3,000 for single people is to be tax-free, the whole problem would be settled.
Social welfare should be replaced by some better formula, for, among other things, Bill C-259 includes social welfare. And social welfare-I touched upon the subject last week and shall say more today-gives rise to crying abuses in several respects. It might be objected that the provinces make the decisions, that the offices are administered by them and that the federal government pays 50 per cent of the expenditures, which is true. However, if the federal government pays 50 per cent, I feel that it should be entitled to control what goes on in some provinces. We know full well that some people are paid welfare allowances whereas they do not need them, and vice versa. That happens in Montreal as well as at home.
On a recent air trip, I met a worker who receives a pension from the Quebec Workmen's Compensation Commission. He gets $86.54 per week; that is the maximum. According to him, it is not enough. So he went to the regional welfare bureau to get more money. He was told he had enough and could not get more but that if he was short of money at the time, he could get an advance, providing he would sign a form stating that he would pay back the money upon getting his next cheque. The worker said he would not sign, that he would find some other way. Therefore he went back home and said to his wife: "Go to the welfare bureau, say I deserted you, that we are separated, that I live with my father, that you are left with our two children and need welfare benefits." His wife complied and went to the welfare bureau. The manager said: "Madam, you are entitled to it." And ever since, they have been paying her $220 per month because of her statement that her husband had left her. Such are the abuses brought about by the welfare system and the same is true of unemployment insurance. Some jobless people, if caught working a few days, are punished by discontinuation of benefits for a week or two. If the person can get away with it, he gets his unemployment insurance benefits. In this way it is a game of hide-and-seek with the welfare system as a whole.
Under the present system, if a person receiving welfare benefits attempts to work he is immediately cut off from payments and if he has worked only a few days, he also comes off badly. So, what does he decide to do? Stay at home without moving, which is an incentive to sloth instead of an incentive to work.

This is the question which must be put.
In my opinion, a national program of social security would eliminate all these expenditures, even unemployment insurance benefits, because an unemployed would get as much in social security payments as he is now getting for other reasons. And he would be allowed to work while drawing an allowance under the social security program.
In my mind, members of parliament, government, people concerned by public affairs should seriously consider the establishment of a program which would help everyone, and not only one category of people at the expense of another.
In English, they say: "Take away from those who have something in order to give to others who have nothing. Take away from the haves to give to the have nots". I say that quite often. "At the end you will have all kinds of have nots and no more haves in this country. And it is exactly what is going to happen".
But we are in a position to vote credits required for the development of our country. It is so true that, as I said earlier, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance confirmed it last Thursday when they announced their program of assistance to municipalities and provinces. We do not object to help being given to the provinces and the municipalities; but we do object to the fact that those billion dollars be equal to a debt towards a few oddballs who have never built anything in Canada, except debts to plunge into debt those who are building the country.
Our party would like to see a responsible government making use of the services of our national bank, the Bank of Canada, which was not instituted for nothing. To date it has not fulfilled its function.
The right hon. Mackenzie King-who in spite of everything, is the spiritual father of all hon. members on the government benches-stated, way back in 1935, that: once a country divests itself of its control of credit and money, it is of little importance who legislates in that country. Once the practice of charging exorbitant interest rates takes command, it ruins any nation! Canada is no exception. This is so true that the more we legislate, the more
(Mr. Caouette.]
we mess about with budgets, and the more we submit mini and big budgets, the more trouble we invite.
It was alleged, last week, that the unhappy state of affairs in Canada and the increase in unemployment during the month of September should be attributed to the 10 per cent American surtax on Canadian exports to the United States. Nevertheless, on the same day, just a few hours later one could read in the Ottawa and Hull newspapers that in spite of the 10 per cent surcharge our exports to the United States had increased by 9 per cent in September. The tax has been in force since and the number of unemployed has increased even then! There is some inconsistency in that.
Mr. Speaker, let us use the services of a bank that was created for us, that is the Bank of Canada. This is not demagogy since it is our bank. Instead of going to the United States, let us go and see Mr. Rasminsky and tell him that the final decision rests with the Parliament of Canada and not the Bank of Canada. It is up to us to decide, and instead of going to the United States to get the one billion dollars we need let us have Mr. Rasminsky print them. This would be better because it would cost us less to create our own credit to finance our school boards, our municipalities and our provinces.
Then, Mr. Chairman, we could say that such a bank would promote the establishment of a genuine social security scheme under which there would no longer be any discrimination against the various social segments of our society. As a consequence, we could guarantee economic security and personal freedom to all. That is what my colleagues of the Social Credit party are advocating, that has been our objective since we have been sitting here and that is why we invite our colleagues to study this program seriously and objectively.
If the Liberal members agree, I am going to vote like them. If the Conservative members also agree, they have only one thing to do: to come and sit among us. Of course NDP members would gain much by becoming Creditistes.
