With respect to social welfare, would not the program advocated by the hon. member create a problem in connection with federal and provincial jurisdictions since some welfare programs come, at present, under provincial jurisdiction and others are under federal jurisdiction?

I suggest the federal-provincial conflicts would be eliminated by the establishment of a national plan. Family allowances and old age pensions in the amount of $80 would come under federal jurisdiction. Then, no province would be opposed to such a program if everyone was treated on an equal footing.
Does the hon. member not believe that the government could then be described as a centralizing power?

No, I do not think that we are regarded as centralists because of the old age security pensions. I readily admit that we will still meet with swelled heads like Michel Chartrand, Reggie Chartrand and Lemieux, from Montreal, but nevertheless our program is of national interest and intended for the whole Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to speak generally about one aspect of Bill C-259 that has not been mentioned heretofore and which I believe is of vital concern to a great number of the Canadian people. I refer to the section of the bill that eliminates the gift tax.
The elimination of the gift tax not only creates difficulties for the provincial governments because of the lack of consultation with them and the loss of revenue it constitutes for most of them, but it is also logical that the capital gains aspect of the bill as introduced-assuming this
Income Tax Act
provision will be passed-be phased in with the elimination of the gift tax to avoid complete disruption for the provinces and also for those people who have been vitally concerned with this aspect under the previous tax laws.
To begin with, I should like to commend the government for increasing the allowable tax deduction for recognized charitable organizations from 10 per cent to 20 per cent. I believe this is a very positive way of providing an incentive for Canadian citizens to participate more directly in many worth-while organizations that come under the category of "charitable organization". I am thinking particularly in this regard of the new "ngo"-non-government organizations-department of CIDA.
It is the policy of the government to allot a certain portion of its budget to this department of CIDA in order to encourage the non-governmental organizations-the private sector organizations-to participate in and contribute to international development. It is rather interesting to note that the private organizations have made a very sizeable contribution to the emergency created by the Pakistani refugees in India at the present time. In fact, as of the end of last month the government itself had directly contributed $6,098,610 to the refugee fund to relieve the disastrous situation in India. Private organizations over the same period of time, according to the records, contributed $1,393,216, though I believe the amount contributed is actually greater than this figure since some money has been sent directly to India without notice being given to the government. In any event, this contribution is more than 20 per cent of the contribution made by the government.
This is the kind of participation and involvement that I think is good, and it is to this end that the ngo department of CIDA was established. I also note in this regard that during this time the provincial governments had given some $370,000, which means that the citizens of Canada have directly donated more than four times the amount contributed by the provincial governments. I am referring only to the amount given for the relief of the Pakistani refugees; there are many other forms of international and emergency relief, not to mention charitable donations to home based projects.
I believe that what I have to say this afternoon is representative of the views held by a wide range of nongovernmental organizations. I do not mention only those organizations that are related to religious bodies, but if I may speak generally may I say I am voicing opinions held by the Jewish Congress, representatives of the Jewish faith, the opinion of the Catholic church and its various organizations coming within the category of registered charitable organizations, and I am speaking also for a broad section of the Protestant churches.
In addition to these religious organizations, I am speaking for organizations such as UNICEF, the Community Funds and Councils of Canada, the Canadian Hospitals Association, CARE of Canada, the National Council of the YMCA, the many associations across the land having to do with retarded children which do a tremendous amount of work on a voluntary basis, and also for the Canadian Institute for the Blind. The gift tax proposals affect a broad range of organizations, and I do not think

October 18, 1971
Income Tax Act
the government has fully realized that its proposals affect this aspect of charitable giving.
In my opinion, the Canadian way of life is greatly enriched through efforts and contributions made by charitable organizations. Many of them provide facilities for education, physical development and research. Many others help alleviate the hardships that often come in the wake of disasters, such as the Pakistani refugee emergency. Opportunities to serve society become available in a way that could not be provided by government, and as a result the government is relieved of many administrative and financial costs that would otherwise have to be provided out of taxation.
I feel that the needs of the Canadian people and of the Canadian government would be better served by encouraging private charity and philanthropy to support endeavours of a philanthropic nature, where otherwise they could become needs that the public would expect the government to meet. It is a rather sad commentary on the attitude that we take to one another today that so many people in Canada regard it as not their responsibility to meet these needs; rather they look to government to meet them. Therefore, I think we should be careful to see that nothing is done that would impair charitable giving; rather, we should provide incentives and encouragement. From this standpoint, the elimination of the gift tax will have an adverse effect.
If the government were required to meet all these needs, I feel that the quality of the services would suffer simply by reason of scarcity of funds. The proposed increase of the permitted charitable deduction from 10 per cent to 20 per cent of the taxpayer's income provided for in Bill C-259 is a great encouragement. However, other provisions in Bill C-259, namely those that impose a capital gains tax at the time a gift or bequest is made to a registered Canadian charitable organization, may very well jeopardize the concept of charitable giving in Canada as we know it. Liberalizing the tax laws of Canada in favour of charitable organizations will result in a very small loss of revenue to the government. However, I believe that the benefits to the community will greatly outweigh such loss and will actually reduce the need for government expenditure and subsidy.
The proposed new Income Tax Act contains several sections that change the present provisions relating to gifts for charitable purposes. One major change is the increase from 10 per cent to 20 per cent of permitted charitable deductions. Unfortunately, the sections relating to deemed realizations on capital gains at the time of a gift or on death do not except gifts or bequests to registered Canadian charitable organizations. I believe that under the old tax laws there probably existed many loopholes of which organizations took advantage to go outside the intent of the law, and I believe that such loopholes should be closed. My comments relate to legitimate charitable organizations, and I recognize that the government has a responsibility to see there is no evasion of the law. Inasmuch as the imposition of the capital gains tax on such deemed realizations was apparently meant to replace the tax received under the estate tax and the gift tax sections of the Income Tax Act, neither of which of course previously taxed gifts or bequests to registered Canadian

charitable organizations, it concerned us greatly that under the proposed new sections the government will not only not be carrying out at least its old views, encouraging charitable giving, but in fact will be severaly penalizing any donors who may wish to make gifts to registered Canadian charitable organizations.
So I would respectfully submit that gifts or bequests made by any person to registered Canadian charitable organizations should not be subjected to a capital gains tax, and further, that the value of such gifts should be based upon the fair market value of the asset as at the date of the transfer. In section 70(5) it is provided that a depreciable property of a deceased taxpayer is deemed to have been disposed of, at a fair market price, on the date of death of the owner. The "amount" realized is then liable to a capital gains assessment. Similarly, paragraph 69(l)(b) provides that the same situation applies where a taxpayer makes a gift of such property to any person, inter vivos, or literally "among the living".
These rules would have a seriously inhibiting effect on a person who wishes to bequeath property to a charitable organization, or who wishes to make an outright gift of it while he still lives. A person making a donation of property which had originally cost $10,000 and which is now worth $50,000, would find himself assessed as though he were making a personal profit of $40,000, 50 per cent of which would be taxable. The raised limit of 20 per cent of income allowable as tax deductible donations to charity, that is to make a gift such as the one mentioned above worth $50,000 and to avoid a tax on $20,000, would require a person to have an income of at least $100,000 over a two year period according to the paragraphs on valuation day produces and capital gains contained in the bill. To fully realize a tax saving on the entire $50,000, a person would need an income of $250,000 over the two years.
The minority report of the Royal Commission on Taxation, the report of the House of Commons standing committee, and the report of the Senate committee on the white paper proposals for tax reform, have some very interesting statements to make in this regard. In these reports a number of unbiased observers concluded that the application of a capital gains tax to charitable gifts of appreciated property would create unfair tax burdens inconsistent with the policy of encouraging such gifts, which has always formed part of Canada's tax system. While a number of donors do make outright gifts or bequests to charities, many others would prefer to irrevocably transfer money, securities or other assets to a trust which would pay the donor or his nominee an income during his lifetime, and possibly to his spouse for her life if she survives him, and on the death of the survivor the remainder would go to a registered Canadian charitable organization.
The Department of National Revenue has interpreted the provisions of the present Income Tax Act to permit a charitable deduction to donors who purchase a charitable annuity from registered Canadian charitable organizations for any excess of the purchase price of the annuity over the amount expected to be returned to the donor. Since this type of charitable deduction is already being permitted by the government, it would not appear to be a
October 18, 1971

large extension of that idea to permit similar deductions for gifts to charitable remainder trusts.
The new Income Tax Act should encourage the creation of charitable remainder trusts, and therefore we would suggest that there should be amendments to Bill C-259 which would permit donors to create inter vivos and testamentary charitable remainder trusts such that the following benefits would accrue: first, that any capital gain on such disposition to the trust should not be deemed as taxable to either the donor or to the trust; second, that the gift value be based upon the fair market value of the assets on the date of transfer; third, that the donor obtain some type of income tax deduction for his irrevocable gift of future interest to the charity; fourth, that the deduction generated be subject to the 20 per cent of income limitation or such other limitation as the government may agree to, and the carry over provision with respect to the unused surplus of such charitable donation be increased from one year to five years in view of the amounts usually involved; and fifth, that the wording of the act be made clear to permit a donor to give appreciated property other than cash.
I think also that it would be wise to allow this new act to encourage a pooled income fund concept which is a variation of the simple charitable remainder trust. Under this method, donors make gifts to a pooled income fund, where it is invested together with gifts of others who make similar life income gifts. The donor receives his share of pooled income fund earnings each year during his lifetime and on his death the remainder of his gift would become the property of the charity. I would suggest that this type of gift have similar tax benefits as we suggested for the simple charitable remainder trust.
Another but a new concept-because what I have just mentioned is really contained under the present legislation but omitted under the new through the elimination of the gift tax-would be provision for a short term trust. Under this method, a donor would be entitled to place part of his property into a trust for the benefit of a registered Canadian charitable organization for a short term, say two to five years, during which time the income from such property would be transferred to the charity and at the end of the term the donor could recall the property from the trust at the same cost base at which the property went into the trust, and then proceed as before. I believe also that it would be very wise if Bill C-259 contained a provision which would extend the carry over provision which at the present time is only for one year but which could well go for five years to permit donors to take full advantage of the charitable deductions.
I believe that these suggestions are much more worthwhile and of much greater significance to more Canadian people than most of us realize. I believe that by adopting such changes the government would continue to encourage a society in which individuals are generous in helping each other, and would be encouraged to give as a means of demonstrating good civic responsibility and in fulfilling their sense of moral responsibility. Therefore, not being able to move amendments of this type when we come to clause by clause consideration, I urge that the government give serious consideration to the implementation of these simple but basic suggestions as they relate to charitable
Income Tax Act
giving. The present law is changed in a negative way in Bill C-259, probably in a way that was not really intended.

I should like to participate in this debate by taking a somewhat more general approach than the hon. member for Red Deer, although the thought behind the proposition that he advanced to the government should be given the consideration it deserves and should result in amendment No. 98 being proposed by the government and placed before the House for consideration. I should like to take a more general approach and go back to the period of time when the government brought forward its proposals in the white paper on tax reform. At that time, it was suggested to the Canadian public that we were going to have a complete reform of taxation in Canada and that, as a result of it, many changes would be made in the taxing system. As we look at the situation today, and as we watched the Minister of Finance perform the other evening, we discovered that from that period until now there has been a very depressing reaction within the business community. It is very easy for the government to say that the 650,000 people who are unemployed in this country are unemployed because of the 10 per cent surcharge or because of some other situation beyond their control.
The very depressing situation within the business community started with the government's white paper on taxation. For over two years, the business community of this nation was put through the wringer. Members of the business community had no idea what would happen. They continued making suggestions to the government, and warned of the great dangers they faced and the difficulty they had in planning their programs. They also pointed out the instability which had been created in the minds of businessmen in this country. The government paid absolutely no attention. It went forward and one did not know from one day to the next what we would have in the way of tax legislation. Certainly, a businessman who wished to prepare himself had no idea what he would have to pay in the way of taxes when the government finally made up its mind concerning what the tax reform legislation would be. So, in June we were pleasantly surprised by Bill C-259 because it certainly is not as damaging as we were originally led to believe it would be. At the same time, however, there are a great many aspects of this legislation which do anything but create confidence in the minds of members of the business community.
I listened with great interest a few months ago to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources when he explained to the House that money for development goes to areas where the businessman can obtain the greatest return and expect the greatest amount of stability. Certainly, no businessman in this nation or in the world could become very excited about Canada as a place in which to invest money during the whole, long searching period in which the government forced the business community to wait while it determined what the tax policy would be. Then, last June the government brought forth its tax legislation. In many aspects it is depressing to the business community. It also limits the confidence that should have been built up at that time because of the very evident signs that the economy is in trouble. But the government
8790

O ctober 18,1971
Income Tax Act
went forward and introduced its capital gains tax, this and that and other things.
Then, after all the period of time in which the government could consider what its tax reform legislation would involve, 97 amendments are slapped before us to be incorporated in the biggest bill which I believe has ever been presented in this House. Regardless of whether or not the amendments were the result of consideration and representations, the bill certainly is not a very stabilizing factor for the business community because, once again, any plans any businessman might have will have to await the consideration of the amendments that are proposed.
I come from the Atlantic provinces of Canada. We must expect the federal government to provide legislation that is conducive to the attraction of capital from all over the world to our area in the hope that we can develop our economy in such a manner that it will produce jobs for the 15 per cent or 20 per cent of our people who will face unemployment this coming winter. There is no way this government will create any confidence in the minds of any businessman in the world community. Certainly, this government will not create any confidence in the minds of any persons in this nation sufficient to encourage them to invest money in any enterprises that would produce employment. Certainly there is nothing about the Minister of Finance or his proposals, whether they be those of the other evening or of last June, or any others, that would create any confidence in the mind of a businessman.
Surely, one of the first steps this government should take would be to provide this country with a minister of finance who would instil confidence in the business community and give the business community a feeling that Canada is a good place in which to invest money. We must have confidence in government planning, and that has been non-existent up to the present time. Every time the government is provided with information by Statistics Canada it has to change its predictions because every time that information is different from what the minister had predicted it would be. It is only common sense that if this is the type of direction we have from this government at the present time, no businessman in his right mind would have any confidence in what the government says or in the way in which it does something. Unless something is done about the finance portfolio and soon, we cannot expect anything more than a greater degree of unemployment in the months ahead. This is the sad and unfortunate fact of life in Canada today. It is very depressing that any Canadian should find himself in this situation.
If we believe it is depressing, it certainly is depressing for the 650,000 unemployed and the additional 100,000 who today are frightened to death because they know that before the winter is over they also will be without jobs. It is a desperate, frightening situation for every municipal government in this nation which has to provide the money to pay welfare to those who are unemployed and are not eligible for unemployment insurance because they have not worked long enough in the past 12 month period. Certainly, the federal government in its time in office has done nothing to produce the money to help these municipalities in any way. In fact, the government has done everything to scare the money away and has placed

additional burdens on the shoulders of these municipalities. It is a desperate situation in which we find ourselves at the present time. It will not improve. It will not or cannot improve so long as the present Minister of Finance holds that portfolio. The sooner something is done about that, the better off everybody in this nation will be. There is no doubt about that.

speechtext: Order. Before I see the hon member for Calgary North, perhaps he and other hon members would permit me to read the proceedings for the adjournment debate this evening.

speechtext: It is my duty pursuant to Standing Order 40, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Macln-nis)-Health-Birth Control-Grants to municipalities and voluntary organizations; the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie)-External Affairs-Conference of Francophone countries-Appointment of delegates, voting instructions.

The House resumed consideration in committee of Bill C-259, to amend the Income Tax Act and to make certain provisions and alterations in the statute law related to or consequential upon the amendments to that act-Mr. Benson-Mr. Honey in the chair.
Mr. Chairman-
Let us hear about justice.

I hope my good friend from St. Boniface will bear with me today, because the last time I spoke and the last time my leader spoke, the hon. member frequently expressed himself from where he sat. I know he is a good member, conscientious and always polite outside the House. I hope he will exercise some restraint inside the House today.
I want to start by touching on two points. The first is what happened here on the night of October 14. I would remind the committee that on June 18 the government presented a supplementary budget. On October 14 the government announced there would be a second supplementary budget. This means, basically, when you look at the tally, that there have been two supplementary budgets in 35 sitting days of Parliament. That fits into the picture presented by the last speaker, the hon. member for Cum-
October 18, 1971

berland-Colchester North. This is exactly what he was warning the country, the government and Parliament about-the uncertainty.
Unfortunately, the government has buried the two minor tax changes presented in the supplementary budget of last June in a 700-page bill of so-called tax reform. For the record, now that we have had a chance to review them, the government has tabled 95 proposed amendments, some of which are rather substantial although others are minor. So in a period of economic crisis in Canada there have been three budgets presented in one session. The Minister of Labour used that in his speech the other night, in supporting the government.
Lunch-bucket Mackasey.

He said that we have the most flexible Minister of Finance since confederation, a man who could move at every opportunity. As I say, during a period of economic crisis there have been three budgets in one session. We will now be spending weeks discussing a revamping of the tax structure and this, basically, will be somewhat of a waste of time. In committee of the whole we are now debating 700 pages of tax reform. If that bill were passed right now, I ask what effect would the supplementary budget, the mini-budget of October 14, have if its provisions were read together with the changes proposed in this bill?
I do not think the Minister of Finance, the parliamentary secretary or their experts can deny that in various provisions the bill basically puts taxes up. I see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance frowning, but if he will give me a few moments I will cite examples of where taxes are going up. If I understand correctly what happened the other night, the government got the country into such an economic mess, with unemployment now up to 7.1 per cent, seasonally adjusted, in some places 8.9 per cent-I believe this is so in the province of Quebec-and more than 8 per cent in the Maritimes, that the ministers said to themselves, "We will have to follow the suggestion of the Leader of the Opposition. We will have to do what he has been asking us to do for months. We will have to reduce taxes." So they came in here and reduced personal income tax by 3 per cent and corporate tax by 7 per cent.
I am not the only one who feels this way about what has been going on during this session, with three budgets. This is a three-budget government. I heard the Prime Minister say during his press conference the other day, "Don't worry. If we find that things change, even tomorrow we will have another budget." The government is going from budget to budget to budget. Things move up and down like the mercury in a thermometer. The hon. member for Calgary South knows that the temperature in that city can change very rapidly during the winter. It can be 30 below and rise to 50 above within a short space of time. This is exactly the way with the government's economic policy; it is up and down all the time.
I listened carefully to the Minister of Labour the other night. He put his finger on the government's trouble. He is a likeable chap. As the hon. member for Yukon said, he is the friend of the lunch-bucket group, the labour group. I have spent some time overseas with him. He has a likeable 24319-674
Income Tax Act
character. There are times when he stumbles onto the truth. This is what he said, as recorded at page 8714 of Hansard, and it is an astonishing admission. I have not seen it written up anywhere. It is not very long. After he had cried about unemployment and talked about what the Bank of Canada and the government were going to do, somebody got to him and he became excited. Somebody said, "Hear, hear," and the minister said:
I happen to be one-
I have heard that expression many times over during my years in this House.
I happen to be one-I am not speaking for the government-
He was very careful because he remembered the cabinet oath and he could see his salary on the line. He did not want to go to the woodshed. Only one minister went to the woodshed.
-I am not speaking for the government but for myself-who feels that never again can we tackle the problem of inflation with the blunt instruments of fiscal and monetary policies.
That is exactly what the opposition has been saying for months during the question period and in numerous debates on the budgets. Now the Minister of Labour agrees.
He said last year that 6 per cent unemployment was courageous.

It may have been, and the Prime Minister said you could take it or lump it. If ever there was a piece of legislation that should be shelved, it is this tax measure, because if you worry the business world and the labour world, you are worrying the whole economy and creating instability across the board. The government should withdraw this tax measure. I guess it doesn't take a lot of brains-
That statement will be printed.
I heard my hon. friend from St. Boniface. He has an open mouth but not an open mind. I hope that when the people of St. Boniface read the debates they will realize and appreciate this.
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, if the opposition would only make sense in what they say, I would be glad to get up and give them a reply. But I do not think what they say is worth it.
You have been told not to say anything.

There is an old expression we use out west, and perhaps they know it in Manitoba: Let us talk about wood. How is your head?
The government should immediately withdraw this bill because again it is creating economic chaos. If there is to be any good come out of what was done the other night by the government and the Minister of Finance, no doubt after hours of debate in cabinet, this bill should be withdrawn. This will put more cold water on the economy. The Minister of Labour was right in saying that we should not use blunt instruments to tackle inflation. That is the first point I want to make.

October 18, 1971
Income Tax Act
I would ask, therefore, that special consideration be given to withdrawing this bill. If the member for St. Boniface feels this is a good piece of legislation and that the policies of the government of ever-increasing taxes will get the economy going, then he does not agree with the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Labour or the front benches. I do not know where he stands, because he is always in his seat.
The next thing that I should like to deal with in connection with the debate of October 14 is the statement of the Minister of Finance which adds to my argument that this bill should be withdrawn because, basically, it is the fourth budget. The Minister of Finance began by saying:
I should like to announce certain measures to deal with the current problems facing the Canadian economy and to sustain and reinforce the growth of production and employment now taking place. In terms of production, employment and prices, the Canadian economy is on the course I envisaged at the time of my June budget, before the United States economic measures of last August were announced.
Let it be clear that all of us agree that with the United States imposing the surcharge and with the problems of our exchange with trading nations, we are in economic trouble. But prior to the announcement of these measures and the actions taken by the United States there was between 6 per cent and 7 per cent unemployment in this country. To date, however, there has been no fall-off in exports: the record shows that they have remained stable-so the surcharge has not affected the economy. If the government wants to hide under the economic umbrella of the United States surcharge and what it has done to our trade, there are no facts to support this. Unemployment is at almost the identical level it was before, and our exports have increased. That argument does not hold water.
This government's policy for the control of inflation has been wrong, Mr. Chairman. As the Minister of Labour said, they used a blunt instrument. It was so blunt it was a sledge hammer and it brought about 7 per cent unemployment. The Minister of Finance continued:
No doubt the explanation is complex.
Of course it is complex. The minister then said that those who are recorded as unemployed include men and women who have lost their regular employment, teenagers and older people. He went on to list the number of people out of work. This was exactly the message that the Prime Minister tried to leave at his press conference, that more women were coming out of the homes and the woodwork and applying for jobs, that everything the Minister of Finance predicted was correct except that they did not realize that more people would be looking for jobs. He said that was the only mistake the government made. Well, it is a pretty important mistake. However, ever since I came to this House governments have been saying that more people have been going to work than previously. The GNP is based on population growth, on wealth growth, on our total economic growth. If the government missed that point, they missed everything-and now they are making excuses.
The third thing the minister said was that the government is going to retrain people. I received today an interesting letter from a university student who owes the gov-
(Mr. Woolliams.]
ernment $2,900 for a grant obtained under the university loans system. He has two degrees but has returned to university because he cannot get a job. He has received a letter from a collection agency giving him seven days to pay the $2,900. I will send the letter to the parliamentary secretary. I am sure he will be interested in it. I called the bank and they told me it was not their responsibility. Now the matter is in the hands of a collection agency and it is between the Minister of Finance and the bank. Unless this student pays within seven days, his savings in the bank will be garnisheed. That is the type of program the government is operating at the present time. What is the use of training people when there are no jobs for them? As the Leader of the New Democratic Party said in that debate, we will be the most overtrained, unemployed nation in the world.
The government must get the economy moving. On the question of reduction of taxes, we on this side of the House go along with the government. True, they poured $1 billion into the economy, but that has to be analysed. The truth is, when they brought in the mini-budget they already had $750 million; so they added only $250 million. A deficit of $1 billion might have some good side affects. When the Progressive Conservative party formed the government and had to face the problems of deficit financing, the Liberal party said, "You have to balance the budget". I hear the hon. member for St. Boniface talking from his seat again. The wind blows and blows and blows!
I want to come to another point in reference to the $1 billion deficit. It may affect our exchange so that our dollar may fall below that of the United States. We will be able to do business with the United States and other countries if our dollar is below par value. The mini-budget is good; there are good facts in it.
Hear, hear!

It may be late, but it is better late than never. But now the government is bringing back a tax bill that will hit it on the head. We are back where we started, if we pass this bill. It is the middle-income group that will pay more taxes under the new bill. If a million people are taken off the tax rolls-I am not sure whether it is a million or half a million-the taxes have to come from middle-income people, because expenditures are continually increasing. Surely that can be understood even by the hon. member for St. Boniface. They are undoing what they tried to do the other night when, basically, everybody with some reservations offered congratulations to the government for listening, after three years of economic stagnation.
I have not very much time left and will have to deal with further points later. But I should like to speak on the question of the petroleum industry. The hon. member for St. Boniface is still talking; he never ceases. He is like a twin debater, but unfortunately his words do not get into Hansard.
Go ahead; read what you have there.

Don't worry about my reading. When I first came to this House members made speeches without reading, but today speeches are read, read, read. The
October 18, 1971

bureaucrats write the speeches for them and members don't know what they are reading. That is why the Minister of Finance is in this mess.
The member for St. Boniface cannot even read.
Quiet, boys, or we will not get to the question of oil before six o'clock.

In its submission to the Minister of Finance, the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada has made a preliminary review of the 1971 tax reform legislation in respect of those provisions which particularly affect the oil and gas business.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I see the hon. member is about to read a document. Before he does so, I must advise him that his time has expired. He may continue if there is unanimous consent. Is there such consent?
Agreed.

Mr. Chairman, I thank the committee. I see we have seven minutes left. The Independent Petroleum Association said this in their submission:
While the full impact of a number of important changes in taxation policy may not be known for some time, our association feels certain matters require reconsideration prior to the enactment of legislation.
The oil and gas industry today is most important for our economy. It is important for the economy of the country generally and for the economy of western Canada in particular. That industry, as will be seen if one checks the figures, is responsible in large part for our favourable balance of trade with the United States. Basically, through that industry we sell a raw commodity: we sell crude petroleum and natural gas-energy-producing fuels needed by the United States in very large quantities. An application has been before the National Energy Board. It may have made its decision, or it may be about to decide. It concerns the export, over ten years, of an additional 2.5 trillion cubic feet of natural gas to the United States. That country is hungry for energy. It needs our crude petroleum and natural gas and by-products of those commodities.
I hope that the hon. member for Calgary South, who I know understands these matters, will bend a sympathetic ear to requests for changes in the legislation, because the oil and gas industry is needed in order to keep other industries healthy. The well-being of that industry is felt through the gross national product of Canada. From that industry comes thousands and thousands of jobs all across the country. I do not have the figures with me, but I submit that $300 million or $400 million spent by that industry of western Canada finds its way to Ontario industries. The oil and gas industry orders valves, pipes, steel and other products. If we keep the oil and gas industry healthy we shall help to keep industry throughout the country healthy, including industry in Ontario and other provinces.
The association in its brief went on to say:
Income Tax Act
We are relieved that some of the provisions of the white paper-
The provisions that were considered by the committee.
-which we felt would present serious problems for the Canadian economy, and for our industry in particular, have been dropped from the legislation.
Some provisions have been dropped and they are glad to note that. The association continues:
However, we are concerned that certain changes in the proposed legislation which seem entirely appropriate have not been made. The areas which still continue to give us concern are as follows-
The first matter giving them concern-this was discussed in my party's caucus when we were the government, and I am sure it is discussed in the government's caucus and elsewhere-is that of depletion. In order to put this question properly before the parliamentary secretary I will read from the association's brief. They put the matter in better words than I could use:
Our association-
The Independent Petroleum Association of Canada.
-continues to feel that the abandonment of the depletion concept as it is generally understood in the worldwide oil industry and its replacement with the concept of 'earned depletion' will not attract the necessary capital to the Canadian petroleum industry.
I pause there. There is not very much competition in the case of companies exploring for and developing the sale of natural gas because natural gas is a continental export. Nevertheless, Canadian companies that are engaged in the development and exploration of crude petroleum are in competition with companies throughout the world. We have been fortunate in this regard. There are periodic ups and downs in the petroleum business, in line With the law of supply and demand. Those ups and downs follow economic and international conditions throughout the world. For instance, supplies of petroleum from the Middle East or from Venezuela may be cut off, and at those times the United States requires from us more petroleum. Basically, however, we are on a quota.
The point I wish to make before six o'clock-I will continue these remarks another time-is that in order for companies that are Canadian-owned or financed by Canadian investments to compete, they should be subject to the same tax laws in Canada as similar companies in other countries. Only that way will companies which are developing oil resources in Alberta, in our north and elsewhere stay healthy and in business. We must recognize that there are fluctuations in the market. Sometimes such companies must continue development in other countries in order to ensure their survival in the worldwide oil development program.
I congratulate the parliamentary secretary for the position he has reached in the House. He is from my city and I think he is a very capable man. I just hope he will take to heart the recommendations of the Independent Petroleum Association's brief. I will have more to say about their recommendations, perhaps not this evening but later in this debate.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

October 18, 1971
Income Tax Act AFTER RECESS
The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, I feel at a considerable disadvantage in speaking on this bill because it is so enormous and complex. A great sheath of amendments has been filed in the past few days. It has been difficult to make an assessment of the bill which is almost incomprehensible to many people much more knowledgeable about such things than I am. This bill assumes great significance, particularly at this time of our changed conditions in face of the American surtax and the mini-budget presented last Thursday.
The tax bill has only passed second reading. We are now only on a general discussion of its clauses. At the moment, large portions of the bill are being rewritten. We can expect this process to continue as more of its provisions are found to be contradictory. The bill will be subject to differing and conflicting interpretations, with some unforeseen results. It may ultimately be self-defeating to the avowed purposes of the so-called tax reform. It really means it is difficult to have tax reform. We can have tax change.
Even if the bill moves quickly through the legislative process, the odds against its implementation seem to have lengthened. The sheer complexity of the bill is staggering. This in itself is a considerable obstacle. Further, Mr. Chairman, new barriers have been erected by the American surtax and American objections to the bill. I think it is very significant that the Americans have possession of the bargaining power with which to make their objections stick.
Certain things in this bill have already attracted the interest of the Americans. Pension funds are required, under the reform legislation, to limit their foreign assets to 10 per cent in order to retain their tax-free status. The Minister of Finance has made the same case for limiting the qualification for lowering the corporate tax on the first $50,000 to Canadian-controlled companies. While we may feel these measures are beneficial to us, they have invited the interest of the Americans. This is of significance. It is one of the things included in the so-called shopping list which was leaked to the Chicago newspaper last week.
The Minister of Finance has denied that there is discrimination. However, if one set of investors is given favourable tax treatment there is certainly discrimination against the other. I do not think many in Canada have "bought" the argument of the Minister of Finance. Certainly the Americans have not. We will see whether there will be any changes in the future.
I wish to specifically deal with the small business deductions. This aspect of the proposed tax changes came in for a great deal of discussion during the hearings on the white paper on tax reform. It was no secret that the authors of the white paper believed that the small business deductions should be wiped out entirely. Indeed, their tables indicated they expected to get the bulk of the money to make up the deficit for lowering the personal income tax from wiping out the small business reduced taxation on the first $35,000 of profit.

It is significant to note that everyone was in general favour of the retention of the reduced rate for small business, including the very large corporations. They all suggested that the small business alleviation was very useful and necessary, even though it was agreed that it should not be available for very large corporations. There was some agreement that some restrictions should be put into the new reform legislation. My criticism is that these have been far too great, larger than necessary and may well defeat the purpose of the small business alleviation.
It should be noted at the outset that the incentive is in fact restricted to an incorporated enterprise and is not available to a proprietorship, partnership or business trust. This is not good. It is one of the weaknesses in the taxation bill now before us. The preservation of the distinction between forms of business enterprise for tax purposes will make it impossible for the courts to look to substance rather than form in many instances, for the form is deemed by the tax statute itself to make substantial differences in tax treatment. I think this is a problem that we have in tax legislation. We do not recognize the unincorporated business, the individual entrepreneur, nearly enough in our economic community.
Generally speaking, the present tax on corporations, regardless of the size or nationality of the ownership, is 21 per cent on the first $35,000 of taxable income and 50 per cent on the excess. The new bill will cause a reduction of one percentage point per year until it reaches 46 per cent. This, of course, has been changed by the minister's announcement of a reduction of 7 per cent only until the end of 1972, when presumably it will revert to 49 per cent unless the government decrees otherwise.
The clauses dealing with small business deductions have been subjected to such rigidly prescribed conditions that it is doubtful they will do the job that this reduced rate was supposed to do. Indeed, it is one of the items in the so-called shopping list which the Americans felt discriminated against them. There are so many restrictions in the tax bill on small business that it seems almost certain that many will not take advantage of it.
Under the new tax rates the small business incentive is significantly less generous than the present low rate, particularly when the annual taxable income is less than $35,000 and where the corporation accumulates its taxable income. For instance, a corporation which recorded earnings of $30,000 would be required to pay $6,300 in taxes, whereas under the new rate it would pay a further $1,450. So the new tax proposals are far less generous than in the past, particularly in light of the proposal to reduce the corporation tax rate from 50 per cent to 46 per cent-at the present time, from 50 per cent to 43 per cent.
It is significant that small business will soon be taxed at the rate of 25 per cent. In an extreme situation it could happen that an otherwise qualified corporation which earned a taxable income of $400,000 in the first year of the new system and paid no dividends would be eligible for $50,000 of small business deduction in that year and no subsequent small business deduction. It would then cease to qualify for the small business deduction. This can be contrasted with the present system where both corpora-
October 18, 1971

tions would be eligible for the low rate of tax on the first $35,000. It is also significant that taxable incomes are important factors in the cumulative deduction account, so that the $400,000 maximum amount would be net of business losses, but would include non-business income and capital gains, which would have the effect of significantly reducing the attractiveness of the small business low rate.
The corporations eligible for the small business rate have been significantly reduced in number. They must be private corporations resident in Canada. They cannot be public corporations or controlled in any manner whatsoever by a public corporation, and they cannot be held in any manner whatsoever by one or more non-resident corporations. A public corporation is defined as one listed on the Canadian Stock Exchange or by definition of the minister.
Mr. Chairman, because payment of dividends can extend the period for eligibility, there will be considerable jockeying going on between not paying dividends, facing a potentially higher capital gain, and not getting further small business deduction on the one hand and, on the other hand, paying dividends, thereby extending eligibility for the small business deduction which potentially reduces the subsequent capital gain, but facing the immediate impact of personal taxation.
The new tax changes basically require an owner to run his business to comply with the regulations so that he can obtain the best tax advantage rather than running his business as an expansionary corporation. In dealing with the matter of so-called ineligible investments, the bill seems to be quite complex. The thrust of the intended procedure is to ensure that the 25 per cent small business deduction is available only where the funds are used to expand business or have been brought to personal tax by dividend distribution. The corporation can no longer be used to shelter excess funds from personal tax unless the excess funds are invested in short-term paper or bank accounts. One major criticism of the bill in this area relates to its complexity so far as small business is concerned. It appears that the small business corporation has most of the accounting difficulty of the larger business, and additional problems in complying with clause 125. What, in effect, is the 25 per cent tax on business income on Canadian-controlled private corporations is arrived at by deductions from the usual corporation tax rate. The tax decreases as the general corporation rate decreases, thus arriving at the 25 per cent figure at all times. It might have been simpler to have taken the 25 per cent tax rate on the small business when the preferred rate ends.
In the clauses dealing with the Canadian-controlled private company which has taken advantage of the small business low rate of taxes, an interesting situation would arise. The complicated formula for the new tax is applicable, but in fact it means that there will be a recapture of the small business deduction benefit previously received, minus an allowance for dividends previously paid. The maximum amount recapturable would be $100,000. It appears obvious that control could change voluntarily by the sale of that control to non-residents, but could also occur involuntarily with the death of a Canadian controlling shareholder who bequeaths his shares to a non-resident heir.
Income Tax Act
The tax would also not become exigible if control were acquired by a Canadian public corporation or if the company itself went public. It would appear that in both these cases subsequent conversion to a private corporation controlled by non-residents would trigger the tax. The apparent intent of these new clauses is presumably to prevent the sale of Canadian companies to non-residents. This required refund of the small business deduction tax savings is likely to depress the price a non-resident is prepared to pay for the shares of the corporation, particularly where the price placed on the shares is close to break-up value.
When taken together with the deductibility of interest on money borrowed to buy shares, it would seemingly place acquisition-minded Canadian corporations in a better competitive position vis-a-vis their non-resident competitors. However, this aspect is one of government policy. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) stated in his budget speech on June 18, "We intend that the small business incentive be available only to Canadians, that it should encourage Canadian ownership of our expanding business. Accordingly, if control is acquired by non-residents, the corporation must repay over a five-year period the tax advantage it has received".
However, it is pointed out that clause 190 appears to apply only to share purchases and that the whole principle of the clause can be circumvented by foreign companies making a purchase of assets. This would create an artificial situation. In addition, we note that to the extent the cumulative deduction account has a positive value, a Canadian purchaser may also be driven to purchase assets rather than shares. We therefore question whether the proposed legislation has done anything except require a sale of assets rather than a sale of shares as far as the United States resident purchaser is concerned.
Mr. Chairman, in the clause related to small business deductions the government has significantly narrowed the small business advantage. It has increased the tax on all those who are eligible from 21 per cent to 25 per cent under the $35,000 profit. Only in the group making from $35,000 to $50,000 profit will there be any significant tax relief, and this group seems very limited.
In effect, under this act the government has substantially reduced tax relief to small business. The effect of clause 125 on small businesses which some years are over $50,000 and some years under is to discriminate against them. If there is in excess of $50,000 in any one year, it cannot be applied against the deficiency in another year. It seems likely that only small businesses which do not intend to grow will be happy with this proposed tax feature. Companies that had a good growth potential might still decide to pay full taxes in order to increase their leeway for future selling.
The clauses dealing with the sale of companies to nonresidents are definitely discriminatory and are viewed as such by the rest of the world. By allowing capital to move freely across our borders we are, in my opinion, improving prospects for Canada's independence far more than by setting up nationalistic barriers to investment. New capital bolsters our economy by strengthening it, and it is

October 18, 1971
Income Tax Act
that strength that will help ensure our national survival. The clause dealing with the sale of small companies to foreign investors, losing tax incentives earned in previous years, seems to me a retrogressive step.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to touch on two aspects of the bill before the committee. One is its effect on co-operatives and credit unions, the other its effect on the farming sector in general. I have spoken before in this House about its effects on co-operatives and credit unions and I do so again only because I am daily receiving representations from national offices of co-operatives as well as from local co-operatives and credit unions in my constituency. Since being here I have yet to receive so many representations expressing serious concern, not simply that less money will be saved by the members of co-ops or credit unions but that co-operatives and credit unions will not be able to stay in business at all or be able effectively to discharge their responsibilities to the people in their community, those who established the credit unions in the first place.
The credit unions in western Canada, and I suppose in central Canada as well, offer an alternative to the regular commercial bank. They do not displace the commercial banking system; in business centres of any size one will see both the credit union and the commercial bank doing business and operating effectively. However, to a very large extent they probably have displaced finance companies in small centres or, if they have not displaced them, have certainly served needs well enough to limit the operation of finance companies, as we use the term, in such communities. If that is the case, then the credit union is saving those communities a considerable amount of money as well as increasing the spending power of the people. For those reasons I become very concerned when the government proposes what is almost a punitive tax in this regard.
I should like to read part of a letter I received from the Langham Credit Union. They say:
In connection with the taxation proposals affecting credit unions, the board of directors of the Langham credit union, at our meeting on October 12, have gone on record as being opposed to the taxation of dividends and guarantee reserves of credit unions.
The board of directors have acted on behalf of the interests of our 1,200 members and ask for your support of our position when the tax bill is being debated.
I also received a letter from the Hafford credit union some 40 miles further to the north, who write in the same vein. I am not going to quote the letter, but it does set out in detail the amount of money they handle as well as the amount of credits which pass to their members. The total savings in this community amounted to $948,062. In terms of business operations these days, that is not a large amount, but this credit union is pretty important to the people of the community because it allows them to use their money to help themselves. This credit union states that its members are quite willing to pay taxes on the income they have, but they do not think that any tax proposals put through this House should prevent their using the money to effect savings.
Consumer and production co-operatives seem even more concerned about how this legislation will affect them. These co-operatives include retail outlets in the city

of Saskatoon as well as the Federated Co-operative which operates refineries, feed mills and lumber mills and manufactures fertilizer. This is a large, producer-oriented organization.
In the House today the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion was asked whether he could do something about Imperial Oil moving refineries from a certain area in western Canada so as to ensure that some development was left in less industrialized areas. As I recall, his reply was that he did not have control in those areas, that he could lend money to commercial organizations such as Imperial Oil-although I do not know why it would be necessary-in order to influence their decision, but that that essentially was the limit of his power. I suspect he was quite right.
However, there is one refinery in Regina which is owned by co-operatives and which will stay in the area. No government will have to bribe it to stay in the area and no law is necessary to force it to stay there, because it is owned by the people of the area and that is where they want it. With their money they built it and it is Canadian owned; we do not have to worry about the Americans, the Japanese or any other country owning it and moving it away.
There is another reason why I find it so difficult to understand the approach of the government with regard to co-operatives in western Canada. If it is employment we want, we want institutions that can employ people and improve their standard of living such as co-operatives, credit unions and credit societies that are gradually built up over the years and can provide this service. It may be that as we carry on with this very complicated and, as the previous speaker said, complex and wide ranging bill affecting a great many people, some changes will be made. But it started out pretty badly and has left a great many people wondering what its objective really is, whether it is to raise money, to please the equitable tax foundation or to cut down the effectiveness of co-operatives as real competitors within our society, because that is what they are.
I should like to say a few words regarding farm taxation as it is dealt with in the bill. One thing about which we are concerned with regard to farm taxation is that the method of taxation does not make it any easier than it is now for the family farm or the individually operated or controlled farm to survive. Some aspects of this bill seem to work against the survival of the individual farm, particularly in the areas of capital formation and the maintenance of capital in the individual farm.
Individual farms are not very strong units in terms of capital formation and the retention of capital; that is, the resources available to them are usually limited. This is demonstrated by the fact that over the years we have had the Farm Credit Corporation lending money to farms and we have had to set up a federal agency to provide working capital for farm structures to enable them to expand to a workable size. This would indicate to anyone who thinks about it that the ability of the individual farm to gather together working capital is limited. The fact that provincial governments have moved into this field from time to time indicates the same thing. Yet the bill takes no
October 18, 1971

account of this fact in its approach to the capital gains tax.
It seems to me that some thought should be given to the possibility of not collecting a capital gains tax so long as the transfer is made within the family from one generation to another. It should be possible to devise a method whereby capital gains tax was not collected so long as the farm remained within the family. If at some point it was transferred out of the family's hands and a realized capital gain was made, the taxing body would be entitled to treat that unit in the same way as any other business enterprise with regard to recovery at that point.
I do not know whether members across the way are as concerned as we are about the continuance of the family farm or the individually-operated farm as against the corporate structure. If they are, they should try to ensure that the tax structure is such that the family farm can survive and continue to operate.
There are two other areas of concern that occur to me, one of which is the basic herd concept. The proposal is to eliminate the basic herd concept, and that is not good. The simple idea behind the basic herd concept was to allow an accumulation of capital in a basic herd because it was difficult for the farmer to acquire in one chunk the amount of capital necessary to put together a complete herd, and this was a method by which capital could be accumulated and a herd built up. It is as simple as that.
I sat with a group on a reserve in Saskatchewan listening to them talk about getting together a couple of hundred thousand dollars to build a herd. The first thing they talked about was management, and the second was money, where to get the money with which to go into this kind of enterprise. We had a system which permitted this kind of accumulation and I cannot understand why it is now thought necessary to tear it down.
The same consideration should be given to the depreciation of farm machinery. I would hope we could continue with the straight line depreciation which permits the retention of gains when machinery is traded back. There may be those who complain because any capital gain that may be made at the time of the trade is not taxed immediately. But I suggest that if we insist that any capital gains be recovered at the time machinery is traded, one of two things will happen-either the capital value of farm machinery as a whole, as well as the investment, will decline or the method of trading farm machinery will be completely altered in the very near future; because it should be obvious that a farmer can hardly pay the income tax on a capital gain of $5,000 when he does not have any actual cash out of the deal.
The alternative, of course, is to buy the new machine at the lowest possible price and sell the old machine outright for whatever it will bring. This would cause a major change in dealership operations as well as farm operations in respect of the purchase of machinery. If this is the government's objective, all right, but surely the government should understand what it is doing and what the net result will be.
These are the few points I wanted to make in a general way this evening. My main point is that by this bill you
Income Tax Act
can change the structures which exist in respect of doing business in the farm sector, you can tear co-operatives down and cause a great deal of difficulty, but it will take much smarter men and a government with a much greater understanding of the needs of the farmer and the rural community to put these structures together again.

Mr. Chairman, not having participated previously in this debate, I thought I should make a few comments at this time on Bill C-259. I join those who have said that the effect of this bill on co-operatives and credit unions will not be good. The government talks about its financial and monetary policies to curb inflation, but why does it have to increase the tax on organizations which are providing services and goods to ordinary people?
Co-operatives and credit unions will not go out of business because of this bill: they will stay in business, but will have to charge more for the goods and services they provide to the people. Probably they will not be in a position to pay the same kind of dividends to people who hold shares in their organizations. This item in the bill is inflationary because the people who use these goods and services will have to pay more for them because the government thinks it will get a little more money by taxing co-operatives and credit unions. I hope the government will take a second look at this part of the legislation which is obnoxious to many people.
A good deal has been said about the size of this bill, its proliferation of material and how it will affect the lives of Canadians. We have had income tax bills before. Probably there were loopholes in the legislation and areas which did not cover all the fields in which the government might collect money. However, rather than bring in this huge monstrosity I think the government might have been wise to consider other income tax legislation and amend it here and there, instead of bringing in this bill which lawyers and accountants say will be so difficult to understand that they are not sure it will provide the benefit or advantage that has been suggested.
Most of us in this House realize from time to time that the people of Canada never have been too happy about paying income tax, because most of us have had people come to us with income tax problems. These people ask us to get them out of a mess with the government, or with the law so they can look their fellow man in the face again. When this legislation becomes law, the courts probably will not be large enough to handle all the cases because no one will be able to understand what is going on.
We remember the feeling people had when a man came to their door with a briefcase and said he was going to charge them with an infraction of the income tax laws. Many of us have had the experience of farmers who wondered whether someone was coming to say something was wrong with their income tax return. This feeling will be magnified as a result of the immense bill we have before us tonight. And even that is not big enough because we understand there are to be 100 more amendments to it. Of course, the parliamentary secretary will realize this is not new in respect of this government. I would like someone to point out how many pieces of legislation have been brought in here in the last five years which have not had to be amended either by the government itself or through the assistance of the opposition. It
