October 18, 1971
Income Tax Act
is about time, with the proliferation of people in the government, that the government could bring in a piece of legislation which would not have to be amended.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is respect for the opposition.

Oh! Here we have the government arguing that the opposition is wasting time, and the parliamentary secretary indicating it is the opposition which improves the legislation. I had thought that with all the parliamentary secretaries and ministries of state there would not be many problems in preparing a piece of legislation.
Here, again, we have a piece of legislation which was mentioned in the budget of last June, and then just last Thursday they had to bring in another mini-budget to fill in the holes because they began to realize this legislation would do nothing for the economy of the nation and that it was necessary to bolster it up. But we know this is not the first time a Liberal government has got our country into a mess. I refer to 1957 when a Conservative government was elected. We found quite a mess in those days. Somebody found the report of the Department of Trade and Commerce and in it was the whole story.
Some of the features which were brought in last Thursday are supposed to be new. But how different are they from the measures the Conservative government adopted in 1957 to clean up the mess they inherited from the Liberal party? We are told about the thousands of people who are to be taken off the income tax rolls. The Hon. Donald Fleming did that in 1959 in order to bolster the economy after the mess we inherited. Hon. members opposite would not wish to remember or think about that.
Why are the farmers in such a mess today? It is because the government did not sell the wheat in the west and told the farmers to diversify. Farmers turned to the production of hogs and chickens and flooded the whole country with these products, with the result that agriculture is in a terribly depressed condition at this time. There are one or two suggestions I should like to make in respect of omissions from this bill, matters which were also left out of the mini-budget of last week. I refer to the fact that in spite of all the representations made by prospective home owners and householder organizations that the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials should be eliminated, this has not been done. I think it is very important that it be done at the present time because despite the announcement last Thursday that the government will be making more money available for the building of houses, the average individual today finds housing too expensive. Steps should be taken to reduce the cost of house building. If the sales tax were removed it would cut the cost of a house by $1,000-just enough to meet the inflation in house building for a one-year period.
According to Statistics Canada, between August, 1970, and August, 1971, the cost of lumber and lumber products went up by 12.3 per cent. What effect will that have on the building industry? It means that a man buying or building a house will have to pay a price that he really cannot afford. There are thousands of people in Canada who cannot meet present mortgage costs even though those costs are spread over a 30-year period. Most of us, Mr. 
Chairman, would be very disturbed if we had to carry the mortgage costs that some of our children have to meet today. If the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials were removed, it would be a tremendous incentive to people who want to buy their own homes.
I remind hon. members that a few years ago the government instituted a $500 bonus program payable to individuals who built their houses in wintertime. A recent survey by Manpower Services Limited indicates that there will be a 23.1 per cent reduction in personnel employed in the building and construction industry this winter. We have a lot of unemployment now, Mr. Chairman, but here is a survey which says there will be a 23.1 per cent reduction in personnel employed in this industry. If the government gave an incentive to people to build their own houses during wintertime, by eliminating the 11 per cent sales tax and offering a $500 bonus, this could have a tremendous effect on the industry and on keeping people employed in it.
There is another suggestion I wish to make. It would cost the government a little money but it is a program that worked in the days when we were in power. It would help some of the people in the building industry whose employment is threatened. I suggest an advertising program urging people to do repairs, plumbing and plastering during the winter months. Hon. members will remember the slogan, "Why wait for spring? Do it now." It was effective. The government should give some thought to reinstituting that program.
I do not think we have enough incentive programs for people to improve their way of life, the service they give, the product they make and the job they do. Many of us are disturbed that production per man in Canada has dropped considerably over the last year or so. In the Ottawa Journal of Friday, June 18, there was an editorial entitled, "Canada Would Be The 47th State." It quoted the views of Robert Bonner, the former Attorney General of British Columbia, who retired from politics and became vice-chairman of MacMillan Bloedel Ltd. He made these points speaking at the University of Western Ontario:
There was a time when Canada ranked second only to the U.S. as measured by gross national product per capita. We are now fourth in world rank by this measure-Sweden and Switzerland having displaced us in recent years.
If we are going to spend as the American Joneses, whom we unconsciously imitate, we should first try to earn as the Joneses do.
Canadian income per capita ranked ahead only of West Virginia, Alabama, Arkansas and Mississippi.
Our productive capacity per individual has dropped and this has had inflationary consequences. I believe that the government should introduce legislation providing an incentive to those corporations and companies which allow employee participation in profits. Such corporations should receive a special tax concession. If an individual knows he is going to get a little more for working harder and producing a better product, in turn his efforts will increase the gross national product.
Corporations would be able to reduce the price of their products or the services they supply. Such a program would create better employer-worker relations. The employee would feel he had a stake in the business. Today we hear many manufacturers complain that they have to
October 18, 1971

take reduced prices for many of their products that are classed as seconds simply because of poor workmanship. This has an adverse effect on their profits. There are companies which operate in this way at the present time, but if the government provided incentives to corporations to allow employee participation it would be a great help in combating inflation, reducing costs and bringing about better employer-employee relations.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, when I look at this bill, see how long we will spend on it-not to mention the 95 amendments tabled by the minister-and realize the number of businessmen, accountants and lawyers who will have to spend weeks and months trying to understand and interpret it, I feel it should be withdrawn. If implemented now, it will interfere with the ideas presented to us last Thursday night, ideas that might do the job that the government has been attempting for so long, namely, get the economy out of low gear.
I agree with the article in the Toronto Globe and Mail of October 15, headed "No Time for New Tax Law." From it I read the following excerpts:
W. A. Macdonald, Toronto tax expert, this week neatly capsuled for the Ontario Economic Council some of the reasons why it would be wiser to put the tax bill back on the shelf for the time being.
For one thing, it is so big and so complicated that only a few experts can ever hope to understand it and even they don't yet. As Mr. Macdonald says, it's ironic that a government which insists that business make everything understandable for the consumer should not give two pins about making taxation understandable for the taxpayer. On this score alone the bill should be delayed for proper assessment.. .
Finally, will the tax bill do anything to strengthen the Canadian economy to meet the pressures created by Mr. Nixon? The answer has to be no. It could damage the capacity of our industry to compete, it could enlarge our problems with the United States, our biggest customer, it would certainly divert vast stocks of both public and private energy to the sterile business of examining the tax structure when that energy is urgently needed on the economic front.
It hardly seems necessary to add that Finance Minister Edgar Benson should do at once what he should have done before- withdraw that tax bill and concentrate all his efforts on our real problems.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Withdraw the bill and then resign.
Mr. Chairman, I sincerely hope that the government will take into consideration the suggestions I have made which I think are important if we are to get our economy back on track.

Mr. Chairman, I would like at this stage in the consideration of this bill to make a few comments on tax reform.
Almost two years ago, the government tabled a White Paper on tax reform. The White Paper and the introduction of the bill before us have not thus been conjured out of thin air. The bulky measure has been in preparation for at least ten years.
Indeed, that measure will have far-reaching effects on our economy. A great number of Canadians will be involved one way or another by the proposed changes. A certain number of persons-allegedly 700,000-will no
Income Tax Act
longer have to pay income tax, which means that since they do not have a sufficient income, the experts of the department have decided to strike the names of those taxpayers off their lists.
On the other hand, new kinds of income will henceforth become taxable, probably in order to allow the government to collect the same revenue. I would be surprised by the contrary.
By the way cuts and additions have been made here and there, I would be surprised if the government were to collect less. I think it will collect more especially because of the new factors included in that tax reform.
Consequently the government is about to collect more. Experts say such is not the case but past experience allows us to believe it will be so.
After the supplementary budget was announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) on October 14-budget that will show a deficit of over $1 billion-the government goes on following the beaten track. Interest rates will be pushed higher by new debts. Consequently, tax receipts will have to be maintained at the present level and perhaps increased. However, the bill now under study will ensure the continuity of tax receipts and everything in the bill has been planned to that effect. I am sure that this objective will be reached.
Since some people had nothing left because they had been squeezed until they were dead broke, it became necessary in order to keep the same level of tax income to impose another group by adding new elements to the tax system. So that was the trick.
In ten years from now, this group called the middle class will be eliminated, because we will then be at the same point we now are. The problem will be very hard to solve. Groups of experts and economists will be at work two years hence, to prepare the next tax reform, which will likely be introduced in this House in the eighties. Then, the middle class will not appear any longer on the list, because it will no longer be able to contribute to taxation. The tax burden will then be carried by the better off people. What we call tax reform is not really a reform at all.
In a speech the Minister of Finance delivered in Toronto on August 26 last, he stated, and I quote:
As I stated in my budget speech, the publication of the white paper has been an important stage in the development of participatory democracy in Canada. Thanks to the debate, the discussion it gave rise to, it has been possible to develop a tax reform program which not only meets Canada's needs but also reflects the views of the Canadian people.
I have received many letters and briefs from individuals, groups of citizens, co-operatives, caisses populaires and credit unions. Having read them, I have a feeling that "participatory democracy" is not functioning very well. I am rather inclined that it is a one way proposition.
I might understand better if the hon. minister were more specific about what he means when he speaks of the "needs of Canada and the Canadian people".
The tabling, by the minister, of 95 amendments to his own bill is another indication that he has doubts, that the proposed reforms are not specific enough, or that they have not been studied in depth. Is it any wonder, then,
8800

October 18, 1971
Income Tax Act
that there should be protests? We cannot expect the people to understand every proposed change, when those who have drafted and considered them for years are "lost" and unable to give straight explanations, especially on the clauses concerning co-operatives, caisses populai-res and credit unions.
In the case of co-operatives, the government has introduced a new aspect in its taxation system, that is the concept of used capital. This new element in the legislation and which applies exclusively to co-operatives and credit unions seems to me to be discriminatory.
Bill C-259 is aimed at burdening co-operatives and credit unions with tax loads similar to those which must be assumed by other kinds of ventures, while they do not enjoy the same advantages. They are submitted to a taxation method which is inconsistent with their nature and which would require, if they wanted to comply therewith, that they renounce their fundamental characters.
Co-operatives and credit unions are unlike other businesses. They do not enjoy the privileges granted to big corporations or to banks, which may mint the credit of society. All that co-operatives have managed to gather is voluntary service.
It matters, at this stage, to recall the elements which distinguish co-operatives from other firms. First, these are firms whose members are owners and users. Then, these are corporations whose members exercise control in a democratic fashion. And last, these are firms whose members distribute the benefits at the end of the year, not in proportion to invested capital, but on the basis of the use of services.
Starting from these three elements, one may say that co-operatives, caisses populaires and credit unions are different from other firms.
Bill C-259 purports to interfere with the internal management of co-operatives and the relationship between the corporation and its members, and this, against the basic rules of co-operation. The tax system to which Bill C-259 will subject co-operatives does not only retain the concept of an arbitrary return on the capital employed for the purpose of determining the income of such institutions; it also gives definitions and proposes a series of provisions which increase the gravity of the consequences of the use of that taxation formula, the latter having no logical basis and being, to all appearances, discriminating.
The co-operative movement has always stated clearly that it is not asking for any preferential treatment, but that it wants co-operative associations to be recognized for what they are. Far from acceding to this request, Bill C-259 places co-operatives and credit and savings unions in an unfavourable position by comparison with companies and other corporations.
When the government proposes, in the case of caisses populaires and the credit unions, that the social capital- which we call social shares-be considered on the same footing as company shares, that is simply arbitrary.
The members' savings called "shares" are, for all practical purposes, demand deposits which may be withdrawn

at any time. In short, such amounts are deposits similar to those committed to trust companies.
As the capital of the caisses populaires and credit unions does not appreciate, there cannot be any capital gains. It is exactly like all other funds deposited with trust and finance companies and banks.
It is no secret that trust companies and chartered banks are accepting deposits in the same way as the caisses populaires and credit unions. Are such deposits subjected or will they be subjected to the requirements which are anticipated for the caisses populaires and credit unions? I do not think so. So, why incorporate these provisions in clause 137?
Contrary to what we are led to believe by the tax reform bill and the minister's interpretation, the caisses populaires do no't need permanent capital to operate. They lend to their members the savings they receive on a day to day basis, or, very seldom, the amounts they are legally entitled to borrow. Therefore, aside from reserves for doubtful debts, they have no capital. They exist solely in order to promote the economic and social interests of their members, whose welfare is their only objective.
Up to now, the bonus paid to members out of social capital was viewed by the government as interest income and reported on T-5 forms, tax being paid by members receiving such interest.
The attitude of Bill C-259 towards caisses populaires and credit unions is arbitrary and anti-democratic. It is flatly taxing voluntary activities of people who for many years have been working without remuneration for these co-operatives, resulting in the accumulation of their present reserves and those of credit unions. Credit unions have been built up through voluntary service and dedication.
I know in some sectors they are viewed with disfavour, which is easy to understand since they do not allow for control and manipulation at will of the savings of the people. Thence the necessity for inequitable legislation to destroy the instruments the people have given themselves, building them up through their work over many years.
For the last 20 years, the caisse populaire in my hometown has financed the construction of some 1,000 housing units while the CMHC has built 53 only. If the people had had to wait until the government provided them with houses, I wonder where we would be today. I do not mention here the various loans granted to businessmen and individuals who would have been required to pay higher interest rates to finance companies which are nothing but branches in disguise of chartered banks.
The caisses populaires and credit unions have greatly assisted thousands of people in Canada and to some of them this help was the stepping stone which has enabled them to solve their financial difficulties and obtain the bare necessities of life. The merits and the part which credit unions have played in Canada are being recognized today across the country to the extent that if they did not exist, it would be necessary to create them.
We must keep in mind that people who put their money in cooperatives or caisses populaires are liable to income tax. There is no question that dividends received from
October 18, 1971

savings organizations should be taxable, regardless of the level at which each member is taxed.
The whole of society will suffer great hardships unless we provide for some adjustment of our tax system to the structures and the unique role of co-operatives, caisses populaires and credit unions.
I have asked on several occasions during this session, on behalf of all Canadians, and particularly of the people in my constituency, for more equitable tax exemptions.
The $1,000 personal exemption is totally inadequate, in view of the price increases to which we have been subjected for the past 20 years.
The bill now under consideration would increase exemptions to $1,500 for single taxpayers and $2,850 for married, taxpayers-which amounts, for all practical purposes, to $29 a week for a single person, and $55 a week for a married couple.
Those amounts are even below the minimum needed to live decently which has been set by the Economic Council of Canada, a governmental body.
The present amounts of $1,000 and $2,000 were set 22 years ago, in 1949. If it took 22 years to economists and top civil servants to achieve such a result, I am wondering how long we will have to wait until a proposal is brought before the House again in order to review the basic exemptions proposed in this bill.
If he really wants to be realistic the minister should review his position concerning basic exemptions and think it over more carefully in order to take into account the present circumstances, especially the cost of living.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a little of the committee's time and make a few points regarding Bill C-259 while we are still on the general discussion. I hope to be able to make further observations when we discuss the bill clause by clause. We are discussing one of the most difficult and complex pieces of legislation that has ever been presented to Parliament. It is immensely complicated. I only read as far as page 8, and anyone who does not think it is complicated need only look at such subclauses as are found on that page of the bill. I think it is worth putting clause 6(2)(a) on the record. It deals with the reasonable stand-by minimum amount charge with respect to the operation of a car and provides as follows:
-where the employer owned the automobile at any time in the year, an amount in respect of its capital cost to the employer equal to the percentage thereof obtained when 1 per cent is multiplied by the quotient obtained when such of the aggregate number of days hereinbefore referred to as were days during which the employer owned the automobile is divided by 30 (except that if the quotient so obtained is not a full number it shall be taken to the nearest full number or, if there is no nearest full number, then to the full number next below it)-
And so on.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there is no simultaneous translation.
Who on earth could translate that?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Explain.
Income Tax Act
I said it was complicated and I illustrated my point by reading part of one subclause.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That should not be beyond the grasp of the average individual.
This bill is tremendously important to the taxpayer and has a great effect on the pocketbooks of Canadians.
It will help to line the pocketbooks of lawyers and accountants.

The new tax system will have tremendous ramifications for us all. Certainly, the new income tax bill is a complex tax structure. In our consideration of this bill we must think of something else, too. This bill was drafted some time ago when the economy of the country was supposed to be moving ahead. Now the atmosphere is entirely different. Our economic outlook is far from good. We are faced with the 10 per cent United States surcharge. We have Great Britain entering the European Common Market and many other economic clouds hanging over us. They were not there when the bill was drafted.
Does the bill fit the present-day situation? If we ask ourselves that question sincerely, we will have to say no, it does not. Beyond the impact of the bill on individuals there is another aspect of taxation which affects the whole economy. That is its capacity for growth in the country, its capacity to adapt to changing conditions in the country and changing conditions in the world. The question we must ask ourselves and the government is, what does this tax package really accomplish in terms of the health of the whole Canadian economy? What do these changes do, for example, to help us fight the battle of massive unemployment and the battle of inflation? What do they do to improve or even maintain our trading position in the world where all the established trading partners are under attack and have been for a long time?
With regard to world trade, what is there in this bill that will take care of the situation of the United Kingdom entering the European Common Market? What about the free trade aspect of this situation? What discussions went on with regard to consideration of the products which we now sell to the United Kingdom? Was any thought given to Canada becoming an associate member of the European Common Market? I doubt whether this bill will fit into the general economic situation when we consider all these categories.
In the short time that is available to me I will restrict my remarks to four or five headings. First, the rearrangement of depreciation on residential apartments or accommodation; second, the concern of municipalities regarding tax reform on anti-pollution devices; third, how this new tax bill will affect the farmers as I see it in my particular area. I will mention one or two examples of the new tax as it affects the taxpayer who thinks he will have a great reduction in income tax. I think I will be able to show that it is not very great. There is also the idea of why some arrangement was not made for the young married couple, for example, buying a home. They are paying principal and interest on their mortgage, and no arrangement has

October 18, 1971
Income Tax Act
been made and no thought given to their being able to deduct the interest payments from their taxable income.
I would like now to make a few comments under each of these headings, Mr. Chairman. With regard to the arrangement of the depreciation on residential apartments, this new tax bill will have no effect other than to raise rents and interest rates. It seems most unfair that the government has changed the rules of the game halfway through. Many people in Canada have invested their money in apartment buildings. They did so because there was a certain money into residential buildings, thereby providing housing or residences which are so badly needed in Canada.
Under this new bill there will be the matter of the terminal tax liability taking place. Each year the depreciation will have to be written off.. There are other facts stated in that clause which are very complicated. I must admit that I do not fully understand them, even lawyers and accountants will have their problems. In any event, it will not be conducive for people to invest their savings in apartment buildings, etc. They will not be keen to do so. It certainly will not be attractive for them to put their money into such enterprises. If this is the case, we will have higher rents and higher interest rates, two things we cannot afford in this country. We want the opposite. We want rents to come down and interest rates to be lowered.
With regard to the concern of municipalities in connection with tax on anti-pollution material, I understand the association of mayors and reeves is quite concerned about this. On June 18 the Minister of Finance said:
To further encourage the acquisition of anti-pollution equipment, I wish to announce the immediate withdrawal of the sales tax on such equipment used in production. This new exemption will apply to all machinery and apparatus which manufacturers or producers acquire to detect, prevent, remove or reduce pollutants of water, soil or air. The exemption will reduce revenues by about $8 million a year.
The municipalities are not to have the same privilege. The manufacturers and producers will be granted a blanket exemption from federal sales tax on all anti-pollution equipment. Municipalities will continue to be granted only a very few specific exemptions. The minister stated that the extension of this exemption to municipalities would create complex problems of definition. It is hard for me to realize why it would create a problem to arrive at a definition as between municipalities and the manufacturers who are going to buy such anti-pollution equipment. It seems most unfair that municipalities are discriminated against.
I wish to say a few words about how this bill will affect the farming community. There are several ways in which this bill will have very serious effects on farmers. Many have already been discussed in the House, but I would like to re-emphasize the extent to which these changes will work to the detriment of Canadian farmers. One general point is that all provisions applicable to farmers as individuals should in principle be applicable to family-held farming corporations. Many farmers have discussed this whole bookkeeping matter with their accountants. In many cases where there is a father and son arrangement, a partnership of brothers or some other family arrangement, they have been told it would be wise to incorporate their farms, there would be certain advantages. The same
(Mr. Hales.]
principle that applies to corporations should apply to the individual farmer.
What about the transfer of a farm within a family, whether by sale or inheritance, without realization of capital gains? This is very important. As I understand it, there is no provision for farms to be transferred within a family, except to a spouse, whether by sale or inheritance without immediate realization of capital gains. This is true of a sale or transfer of a farm to a son, or inheritance of the farm by a son.
We have been informed that this problem can be avoided in many cases by good estate planning through incorporation of a farm, and this may well be so. But even in such a case the death of a son, who would be the holder of common shares in an incorporation, prior to that of the father could result in realization of taxable capital gains while the father was still in active charge of the running of the farm, creating severe financial problems. There would be no alternative but to call an auction sale and sell the pure-bred herd which had been developed over the years and handed down. Now this kind of legislation comes in and there is no alternative but to fold up the whole works and call an auction sale.
Apart from this, I do not think it should in all cases be necessary for a farmer to incorporate in order to achieve stability and continuity of the farm business within the family. Payment of tax on capital gains out of the tied up assets of an on-going family farming operation could, and probably would be disruptive. I would strongly urge that the transfer of a farm to the son or daughter of a farmer, whether by sale, gift or inheritance carry with it no realization of capital gains at that time but that in later disposition capital gains be calculated on the basis of the evaluation initially established for capital gains purposes.
There is another clause in the bill which states that a farmer must be in residence on the farm during each year for which he qualifies for the $1,000 farm exemption option. There are real problems here. One only has to look at farming practices in western Canada and elsewhere. Some people do not have their principal residence on the farm; for reasons of the education of their children or other social amenities they live in adjacent towns or villages. This is especially prevalent in the prairie provinces. It should be possible, for years in which a taxpayer is engaged in farming, to utilize this option even if he is not resident on the farm. There are many problems which evolve from this. A son might be using the farm home while both he and his father work on the farm; the father might be retired and living off the farmstead while the farm continues to be worked by the son or hired help. There are many cases where this practice is prevalent.
The question of the basic herd has been discussed very thoroughly here tonight so I do not propose to take up the time of the committee other than to say that a farmer's capital investment in livestock should be treated as capital investment, and the only way in which this can be done is the way in which it has been done in the past, on the basis of a basic herd. Then we come to valuation day. When the value of the herd is to be established there are many things that come into the problem. It may be the
October 18, 1971

time of year when the herd is not in its best condition, it may be a time when markets are at a low point, or it may be a time when the cows are in calf. All these things come into this question and create problems.
Then we have the matter of straight line depreciation. This is to be discontinued. Under the present bill, suppose a farmer bought a tractor for $10,000 and wrote it off down to $5,000; it appeared on his books as $5,000 and he traded it on a new one and a dealer allowed him $6,000 for the tractor. That $6,000 is not taxable under the present bill. Now he does not enjoy that option. He is to have a diminishing depreciation balance system which means, in the same circumstances, that with a $10,000 tractor he depreciates it to $5,000, trades it in and gets $6,000 for it, so he will have a gain of $1,000 and that $1,000 will be treated as capital gain. I do not think the farmer realizes that this is the situation he will face.
The first time he realizes what the government has done to him by changing straight line depreciation to the diminishing balance system will be when he trades his tractor for a new one. I think this is most serious, because farming is an operation which has to keep improving due to technological discoveries and inventions and with new machines coming out all the time. He has to replace his machinery frequently and this new tax will be a very serious handicap for him.
Many people think there is to be a great cut-back in taxes for Canadian taxpayers. I have considered the case of a married person with two children and an income of $8,000 a year. Under the present bill the tax would be $1,215. Under the new bill it will be $1,089. This is a reduction of $126 a year. Divide 52 into that amount and you get a cut of about $2.40 a week in income tax. This is a pretty small deal. It would pay for about five gallons of gas and he would burn that much up in no time going to and from work. So $2.40 a week is not much of a reduction. That is the way the working man looks at it-what comes off his weekly or bi-weekly cheque. When he sees about $2 a week taken off, he is not likely to be very enthusiastic about the new bill.
Take a single taxpayer getting the very minimum, or what we call a breadline wage of $1.50 an hour. He will be obliged to pay tax. He was paying a tax of $230 a year. Now that is to be cut to $204, a saving of $26 for a whole year. Divide that by 52 and you get a reduction of 50 cents per week. So it is not as attractive as we have been led to believe.
I do not know why provision was not made to take care of young people who are buying a home and struggling to pay off the mortgage. Principal and interest payments fall due every month or every six months, yet no thought has been given to allowing taxpayers to write off mortgage interest as part of their expenses, as is allowed business. I do not understand why.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. member. I do so to advise him and the committee that his time has expired.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Carry on.
Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the unanimous wish of the committee that the hon. member be allowed to continue his remarks?
Agreed.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I shall trespass on the time of the committee for only a very few minutes. As I was saying, I cannot understand why that was not done. Business is allowed to write off interest on mortgages, yet no similar consideration has been given to the position of a family buying a house. I cannot understand why this matter was not given consideration.
I shall conclude by saying that I think the minister has two things to consider and decide. Let me make two recommendations. First, this vast volume of 707 pages, weighing 5 pounds 14 ounces, should be divided into the portion that it is essential to complete by January 1, 1972. I think it is an imposition on the House to ask us to complete the whole bill in a thorough and a comprehensive way between now and the end of the year. It would be much better for the minister to pick out those sections that he feels should come into operation on January 1, 1972, and let us deal with them.
Second, I think the minister should give serious consideration to postponing the bill in view of the economic climate in this country and in the world in general. Now seems to be the wrong time in our history to bring in a revision as comprehensive as this to the tax structure of Canada. It would be much better to wait until the economy settles down and we know where we are going and what the future has in store for us.
In closing I should like to read two or three questions asked in a letter that I received today:
Mr. Benson claims the economy is moving ahead at a fast rate. If so, why are so many municipalities complaining about their heavy welfare costs?
Mr. Benson claims an unknown quantity of persons have joined the work force and given a false picture of the unemployment statistics. If this is the case, again, why are the welfare rolls so inflated? Can it be that a vast majority of welfare recipients are not destitute and in need of welfare?
Mr. Benson reduces taxes after stating the government is ever watchful and take measures when needed. If this is the case, how did he bring down a program on the same day as the statistics were released? Are they satisfied with 7 per cent unemployment?
The government, just a few weeks ago, proclaimed the "winter works programs were wasteful and not effective". Why have they now brought down a program which dwarfs all other "winter works programs"?
It would seem to me the Liberal government are incompetent and arrogant and care little for the economy except as a political tool. Frankly, I am quite worried about the future and feel that we are in for a great deal of economic trouble unless we do something without weighing the political consequences first.
These are some of the sentiments of worried Canadians.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with interest to my hon. friend and was tremendously impressed by what he had to say, as I am sure were hon. members opposite. However, as I have listened to what has been said by members on this side I have noticed that not one member on the government benches has risen to challenge the

October 18, 1971
Income Tax Act
collective wisdom that has issued from this side of the House. If one member on the other side had had the courage to rise, I would have expected him to say something about the comments that have been made on this side, so we must take it for granted that hon. members opposite accept with some concern what we have been saying but have not the courage to admit it. I am afraid that when they come to vote they will follow the party line, as usual, and I regret this very much.
I was impressed by what the hon. member for Wellington had to say. He thought one thing the minister might do is to withdraw the bill. I would go one step further and say that he should withdraw the bill and resign, though I do not say necessarily in that order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Do you think you would get any support for that proposition over here?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes, I think there is quite a bit of support for that proposition over there, but the fear of political liquidation that faces hon. members who would sometimes like to express their views prevents their doing so. After all, there may yet be a few changes in parliamentary secretary positions, and a few ministers of state have yet to be appointed.
I refuse to be distracted by comments from hon. members opposite, let me return to my thought about the minister resigning after he first withdraws his bill. I thought of the nearest literary similarity to this, which is found in "A Tale of Two Cities", when at the end of the book Sydney Carter walked to the guillotine. As he did so he said: "It is far, far better thing that I do, than I have ever done." Cannot we visualize the Minister of Finance ascending the steps of the political guillotine, clutching his withdrawn bill to him and uttering those tremendous words?
We like the Minister of Finance, he is a fine fellow, but as a minister he has been an awful disaster, a catastrophe. We know it, the country knows it and I think some of his colleagues know it. If he would withdraw the bill and resign, he would still have a place left for himself in the hearts of the Canadian people.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: You are biased over there.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
No, not biased; I am being completely objective in making that statement. I should like to say this about the bill, though we will be given an opportunity to deal with it in more detail when we enter clause by clause study. In view of the hour I must speak until ten o'clock, because we certainly do not want the vote on third reading tonight. The essence of a tax measure should be simplicity and equity, and this bill fails dismally on both counts. As far as the wording is concerned, I could read some of the bill's provisions which were referred to by the hon. member for Wellington. However, there is no doubt in my mind that what has happened here is that although there are a very few elements of tax reform, the people in the department, operating through the minister, have smuggled into the bill a large number of administrative decisions to make easier the administration of the bill, and at the expense of the poor harassed taxpayer. That is the end result of most of the changes that are envisaged.

We are told by those who are on the bridge of the Canadian ship of state to be calm, to be reassured, not to worry or fret, because all that has happened was known and was predictable; that we are in fact following a scientifically charted course that will lead us away from the abyss to the highlands of safety and security-what is known as the "Benson Big Rock Candy Mountain". What nauseating nonsense, Mr. Chairman!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: You said it; it is your speech.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
It is not only the people who are the elected representatives who are taking this course, those who have been chosen through the elective process to run the show, but their advisers, the modern witch doctors who are the new high priests at the altar of scientific economics, those who daily deal in the esoteric mysteries of predicting the course of human economic affairs. To these we have built great temples in Ottawa, and as they utter their incantations and follow their daily rituals, having looked deep into the holy vessels of their trade, they tell us what do to, how to do it, what will come to pass, when it will come, when we will go to the bathroom, what we will do when we get there, and how long we will stay. This is the kind of advice we are now getting from the economic advisers to the government.
If they should be out in their calculations, do they and their political masters accept the blame? No, of course not. Our employment figures are higher than they should be. Who is responsible? It is all those wretched and ungrateful people who insist upon working but are not supposed to work. They are the women who succumb to social pressures, as was indicated by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration; those ungrateful women who, instead of staying home as they are supposed to and being a statistic according to the statistics of the minister and his advisers, want to go out to work because they have to make a living and supplement the incomes of their husbands in order to make ends meet. That is the reason-
Are you against that?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am for it, but it is the ministers, the government and the Prime Minister, who should know better now. In their statements they have said that the unemployment statistics are unexpected because these wretched people insist on working. This is the kind of drivel which we are being handed.
Then there are the young people who, unable to pursue their training because of financial difficulties, want a job. When these people do this, when they refuse to be statistics within the level of the statistical information furnished, it is enough to make a bureaucrat give up and want to quit his job. They are the masses who do not respond to what bureaucrats want them to do, who refuse to accept their position in the statistical scenario which has been written, and who insist on their right to work because there is more dignity and honesty in a job than in being an unemployment statistic.
It was this government or its predecessor of the same party, with the advice of the same people, which said in
October 18, 1971

1965, "We must pay the Seaway workers an increase of 30 per cent," which set in motion an inflationary trend which did so much to destroy the economic life of this country. It was this government which said to us that with medicare and the pension plan our troubles were over, and now gives us the same bland assurance about unemployment insurance, a new labour code, a new competition act and a changed incidence of family allowances. They say that when these are passed we will have arrived at the milleni-um. What garbage!
Each time our great prophets solemnly and pompously told us that, and for a short while we accepted it; we had some belief in their hypotheses. But then the people began to wonder. They found it difficult to believe that the last few years would have left such a record of hopes blighted, of promises broken, of near disasters, of high intentions frustrated and low intentions consummated if we had been guided by other than error and mistake.
This reached its consummation when last Thursday the Minister of Finance and his fellow wanderers in the economic desert who do not have a chart and do not know how to look up at the stars made a statement in the House as to what their intentions were. Everything they had stood for, every premise which they had laid down, every cardinal economic philosophy which they had accepted was discarded when they did the greatest about-face in recent history.
Try to be objective.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Many people have changed their minds, and it is proper they should; but none has left such a slimy trail behind him as the Minister of Finance in what he did last Thursday. Just one week before, the Minister of Finance and his colleagues-not only his discredited colleagues-has spoken against a positive program of tax reduction and industrial stimulation and incentive and had voted against it. I will not take the time, and even if I had the time the rules would probably prohibit me from going into greater detail, but on Thursday, October 7, there was a motion for discussion and a question for decision in the House which laid down a program of stimulating the economy, of providing for tax cuts and incentives, the sort of program which members of this party and of the party to my left had been pleading that the government embrace but which was rejected out of hand by the government which voted against it. The Minister of Finance, his parliamentary secretary and the Minister of Agriculture all voted against it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Your timing is lousy.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It is precisely the same thing which one week later they brought to the House and with great, pompous assurances said, "This is what the government will do". How can anybody have confidence in a government composed of people like that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Get up and cheer, Jed. Don't criticize the opposition like that.
Don't get partisan.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have much more to say. I simply want to repeat what I started out with on the same high, objective
Income Tax Act
level, that it is about time this government reviewed its position, assessed its intentions and said to the people of Canada that there may well be a need for tax relief and a need to deal with these other issues of which I have spoken, but the primary issue in this country today is to provide a climate and incentives which give effect to the instinctive human inclination to improve one's position. In that way, with the kind of incentives we need, this country may indeed move ahead and get out of the slough of despondency which this government has brought upon us.
Even at this late date, if the government really intended to do that, I am confident they would get the kind of support on this side of the House which would be necessary for a program of that kind. But we cannot believe the government, we cannot have confidence in it, nor can the people of Canada, when we consider the type of antics in which they have engaged.
I will suspend this part of my address and leave more severe castigations, in which I intend to engage at a later date, in the hope that the government will give some heed to what I have to say and will decide to act in a reasonable and moderate way to bring back to this country the kind of economic climate which it is entitled to have.
Question.
Mr. Chairman, it would be a shame to spoil a good speech by starting so late this evening. With your permission, may I call it ten o'clock?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has my permission. If he has the permission of other hon. members, we may call it ten o'clock. .

Agreed.
Progress reported.
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 40 deemed to have been moved.

HEALTH-BIRTH CONTROL-GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES AND VOLUNTARY ORGANIZATIONS
speechtext:
['Mr. Speaker, I should like first to thank the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) for his effective contribution to the Francophone countries throughout the world and I hope he will continue to support the assistance that the government is providing to the Francophone states.
Following an invitation from the Secretariat of the Cultural and Technical Co-operation Agency to the Second General Conference of the Agency, the government appointed a delegation to represent Canada at that conference.
That delegation was headed by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier), and I had the great honour to go with him. It also included ministers and officials from the governments of Quebec, New Brunswick, Ontario and Manitoba as well as federal public servants. A press release was issued last October 8 on this subject matter. As regards the vote, that question did not come up at this conference. Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10:16 p.m.', 'Tuesday, October 19, 1971']

maintopic: HEALTH-BIRTH CONTROL-GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES AND VOLUNTARY ORGANIZATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I referred the other evening to a grant of $25,000 made by the Department of National Health and Welfare to an organization called Serena which uses birth control measures with a 25 per cent failure rate. What I tried to find out from the minister was whether similar grants would be available to municipalities and voluntary organizations using methods with proven lower failure rates. Instead of simply answering my question, the minister went into the filter-down theory under the Canada Assistance Plan and indicated his refusal to accept my statement that Serena has a 25 per cent failure rate. This may have been because I made an error and said 24 per cent, but I doubt it.
The minister's rejection of the 25 per cent failure rate figure is curious because it was taken from a survey made

October 18, 1971
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
by a special committee of eminent physicians named by the minister himself. On page 6 of the report, the preface of which is written by the minister, appears the following paragraph:
The contraceptive effectiveness of the rhythm method, if correctly taught, understood and consistently practised, especially if the temperature rhythm method is used, could achieve a low pregnancy rate of 1.8 per 100 women per year. However, statistics show that, possibly because of irregular cycles, or inexpert and careless timing, the result is a pregnancy rate of 25 per 100 women per year.
My question did not refer to what could be in the statistics; it referred to what actually is. The minister appears to be very forgetful in the matter of this report. I think he is also very forgetful of the great need to promote birth control on a large scale in Canada now. The report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women, published almost a year ago, stated that in Canada families with higher education and in higher income brackets have had easy access to birth control methods. The poor and less educated have not. They also want an opportunity to plan their families. The principal responsibility for disseminating information on birth control methods rests with the health and welfare authorities.
The report recommends that the Department of National Health and Welfare do two things. First, prepare and offer birth control information free of charge to provincial and territorial authorities, associations, organizations and individuals. Second, give financial assistance through national health grants and national welfare grants to train health and welfare workers in family planning techniques. What has the department done? This is what I have been trying to find out for some time. In September I put questions on the order paper asking what organizations had been given grants for birth control activities and how much each had received, what organizations had been turned down and how much money they had wanted, what organizations are still being considered and for how much they are asking. So far I have had no answers.
Last week I asked if, in view of the $25,000 grant to an organization with a 25 per cent failure rate, other organizations with a proven lower rate of failure could get similar grants. I hope I can get an answer tonight. This is a serious matter for thousands of women and men across Canada who need access to hospital clinics, municipal health centres and premises of various other kinds where they can get the knowledge and the contraceptive means to plan, space and limit their families.
What the minister has done so far-that is, to the best of my knowledge-is to provide a total of $125,000 for birth control purposes throughout Canada. This is tokenism. So long as he does not take this matter more seriously we are bound to see the rate of abortions, legal and otherwise, remain at unnecessarily high levels, and there is no use pretending otherwise. The only way to bring that rate down is to provide birth control knowledge and contraceptives. The initiative in this campaign which the provincial and municipal authorities must share rests squarely on the shoulders of the minister.
Once again I ask my question: Are organizations with a lower failure rate-lower proven failure rate according to

the minister-given access to grants similar to the $25,000 grant that was given to Serena, an organization with a 25 per cent failure rate?

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Ouellet (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: HEALTH-BIRTH CONTROL-GRANTS TO MUNICIPALITIES AND VOLUNTARY ORGANIZATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the hon. member's comments I would like to reassure her as to the intentions of the government with regard to birth control.
It is a fact that the Canadian government intends to subsidize those organizations dealing with family planning. It has already been doing so for some time. The government has also indicated that it would contribute to an international program to help those countries that want to set up family planning services.
I would remind the hon. member that until now the government has made a grant of $100,000 to the Canadian Family Planning Federation.
It is also true, as the hon. member pointed out, that the Department of National Health and Welfare has made a grant of $25,000 to Serena, a birth control organization, to help it finance the printing and distribution of information on family planning.
I would like to call the hon. member's attention on a paper by Mr. R. Tietze, entitled "Ranking of Contraceptive Methods by Levels of Effectiveness" and submitted in 1971, in Boston, to the American Association of Medical Specialists in Family Planning, in which he classifies the sympto-thermal method as one of the most effective. This method must be distinguished from the calendar method. In proof of this, Messrs B. Vincent and associates have prepared a report entitled "Review of Temperature Methods in Contraception" which indicates that one failure occurred in 17,500 cycles. The method used for this calculation is as follows: 1,200 cycles are equivalent to 100 woman-year cycles. It is therefore found a 0.1 failure rate per 1,000 woman-year cycles. An international study mentioned an experiment conducted with 195 Canadian couples using this method. No pregnancy occurred over 1564 months.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-CONFERENCE OF FRANCOPHONE COUNTRIES-APPOINTMENT OF DELEGATES, VOTING INSTRUCTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after the Dickensian, Demosthenesian and biblical statement of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), I feel like a minor prophet. The question which I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) on October 12, the reply to which prompted my intervention tonight, was not my first inquiry concerning the conference of Francophone countries.
On October 1, I asked the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) some questions on the conference. On that same day he intimated to the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) that as soon as conveniently appropriate a statement would be made in the House. So far, Sir, we have not heard that statement in the House. It is regrettable that confusion and misunderstanding should
October 18, 1971

be allowed to develop on this matter because of failure to communicate but, as is so often the case, we must depend on statements made outside the chamber, or made by ministers in other jurisdictions, for information on matters of vital concern to the Parliament of Canada.
A Canadian Press item of October 9 indicates that after negotiations between the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Cultural Affairs of Quebec an agreement had been entered into which gives Quebec the status of a participating government. I quote:
This gives Quebec the right to a separate delegation at the conference, a veto in matters under its jurisdiction and the right to participate wholly in all the institutions and administrative councils in the agency.
There are a number of interesting questions which arise from this statement. In the first place, one wonders by whom the judgment would be made as to whether a matter discussed at the conference would be under federal or provincial jurisdiction. One asks, further, about the role of the other provinces in Canada. Have they sought participating government status? If they have not, and this would appear to be the case, what is their position in reference to matters which in administration are under provincial jurisdiction? Does one province, namely, the province of Quebec, speak for all of them? Is it the sole custodian of French language rights?
As I walked past the centre block on the day the conference was held, I noticed that five flags were showing as symbols of people of this country-the flag of Canada, the flags of Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec and New Brunswick. Although I did not detect the New Brunswick flag, I presume it was there. I saw all the others.
Another matter on which there has been too little information, although it has been sought, concerns the appointment of the delegations. Presumably the "participating" government of Quebec would appoint its own delegation. Would the provinces other than Quebec have any role in naming the rest, or are they appointed by the federal government and do they form a part of the federal side of the representation when the conference gets under way- a conference, we must remember, of sovereign states?
Another matter which should be considered is the role of those other provinces which have Francophonic people within their bounds and for whom the provinces are carrying out programs in the extension and development of French language institutions. Are these people and their provinces without voice altogether at the conference of the Francophonic countries?
I still believe that the one area in which the competence and jurisdiction of the national government must be clearly supreme is in the field of international affairs. Divided jurisdictions and internal vetoes within delegations are in
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion fact a diminution of this sovereignty of the national government. We may for the sake of harmony be as euphemistic as we can about the terms we use to describe the arrangements, but nevertheless there has been a significant diminution of this government's role in the external affairs field.
Regrettably, this has been accompanied by a degree of confusion which cannot be helpful to the Canadian image. In the last two or three years we are developing abroad the impression that we are a country which makes a poor job of handling its own economy. It is to be hoped that we will not continue to rub off the lustre of bur international reputation by poorly conceived and awkwardly executed arrangements to solve internal intensions through the external field.
Even at this late date I ask the government to be forthcoming, to tell the people and their parliamentarians what is going on. Let the truth be told, let the record be set straight, let the information be revealed. These recent exercises in indirect discourse and secretive arrangements can do nothing but harm to this country.
It ill-behooves a government once dedicated to participatory democracy to be so unwilling to divulge techniques whereby the nation's external face is being altered. The creators of Information Canada surely should tell the story of our changing external profile even at this late date, and I invite a full statement on this disquieting matter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like first to thank the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) for his effective contribution to the Francophone countries throughout the world and I hope he will continue to support the assistance that the government is providing to the Francophone states.
Following an invitation from the Secretariat of the Cultural and Technical Co-operation Agency to the Second General Conference of the Agency, the government appointed a delegation to represent Canada at that conference.
That delegation was headed by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier), and I had the great honour to go with him. It also included ministers and officials from the governments of Quebec, New Brunswick, Ontario and Manitoba as well as federal public servants. A press release was issued last October 8 on this subject matter. As regards the vote, that question did not come up at this conference. It is provided that Canada will vote following consultations taking into account the interests of the provincial and federal governments. No difficulty is therefore expected in this regard.
